    Curriculum designTyped Interfaces

    The complete design for a book-style TypeScript + React curriculum, taking a JavaScript developer from "Why does TypeScript exist?" to professional TypeScript + React engineering.

    On this page
    • Read in this order
    • Legend
    • Keeping it consistent

    16 parts · 99 chapters · 783 lessons · 16 checkpoints · 20 projects · 3 capstone tracks, published as three Books:

    Book Parts Chapters Outcome
    One: The TypeScript Language I–VI 1–33 "I can think in types."
    Two: Building Interfaces with React + TypeScript VII–XII 34–76 "I can ship a real app." ★ Essential core complete
    Three: Mastery XIII–XVI 77–99 "I can lead, design, and scale."

    Keeping it consistent

    Sections 11, 12, and 13 are generated from the chapter cards in Sections 5, 7, 8, 9, and 10. After editing a chapter card (title, sections, difficulty, tier, or folder), regenerate them:

    node curriculum/_generator/generate.mjs

    The generator also checks that chapter and section numbering is contiguous and that folder names match chapter numbers, and it fails loudly if anything drifts.

    Section 1Book Vision

    Working title: Typed Interfaces — From "Why TypeScript?" to Professional TypeScript + React Subtitle: A guided journey for JavaScript developers

    On this page
    • 1.1 What this book is trying to accomplish
    • 1.2 The promise to the reader
    • 1.3 Who the book is for
    • 1.4 The shape of the book
    • Why three Books?
    • 1.5 The storyline that runs through the book
    • 1.6 What makes this book different
    • 1.7 Tooling baseline

    1.1 What this book is trying to accomplish

    This book takes a developer who already writes JavaScript and turns them into someone who can design, build, test, ship, and maintain professional TypeScript + React applications, and who understands why each tool, feature, and pattern exists.

    It is not:

    • a documentation index (the official docs already exist and are excellent references),
    • a cheat sheet or feature list,
    • a "learn the syntax in 30 days" course.

    It is a textbook with a storyline. Every chapter exists because the previous chapter left the reader with a problem the next chapter solves.

    1.2 The promise to the reader

    By the end of the book, the reader will be able to:

    Capability Evidence
    Explain why TypeScript and React exist and what they cannot do Can teach the "compile time vs runtime" boundary to a colleague
    Model a domain with types so that illegal states are unrepresentable Uses discriminated unions, branded IDs, and derived types naturally
    Write reusable, type-safe abstractions without over-engineering Builds generic utilities, hooks, and components, and knows when not to
    Build real React applications: routing, data fetching, forms, auth, state architecture Ships a full React + API application
    Treat runtime data as untrusted and validate it at every boundary Every network, storage, env, and user-input boundary is parsed, not cast
    Test at the right level, and know what types catch versus what tests catch Unit, component, integration, and E2E tests with type-safe mocks
    Ship to production with attention to performance, accessibility, security, and observability Production checklist applied to a complex dashboard
    Work like a professional: architecture, libraries, monorepos, code review, team conventions Capstone in a monorepo with shared typed packages and CI

    1.3 Who the book is for

    Primary reader: a JavaScript developer (student, bootcamp graduate, junior or mid-level engineer) who:

    • is comfortable with modern JavaScript (functions, objects, arrays, modules, promises, async/await),
    • has seen TypeScript or React but feels they are "copying patterns" rather than understanding them,
    • wants to become productive and deeply competent.

    Secondary readers:

    Reader How the book serves them
    React developer who never adopted TypeScript Reading path that skims Parts VII–VIII and focuses on Parts II–IV and IX onward
    TypeScript backend developer moving to the frontend Reading path from Part VI straight into Part VII
    Experienced developer refreshing fundamentals Checkpoints let them test out of parts quickly
    Aspiring library author or framework developer Book Three (Advanced and Professional) and the library capstone track

    Not assumed: prior TypeScript, prior React, a computer science degree, or backend experience. Assumed: JavaScript fundamentals. These are verified in the JavaScript Readiness Checkpoint and not re-taught.

    1.4 The shape of the book

    The book is one continuous journey published as three "Books" (volumes). Each Book ends at a natural stopping point where the reader has a coherent, usable skill set.

    BOOK ONE — THE TYPESCRIPT LANGUAGE                    "I can think in types."
  Part I    Why TypeScript?
  Part II   TypeScript Foundations
  Part III  Thinking in Types
  Part IV   Generics & Type Transformations
  Part V    The TypeScript Toolchain & Ecosystem
  Part VI   TypeScript on the Server & at the Boundaries

BOOK TWO — BUILDING INTERFACES WITH REACT + TYPESCRIPT   "I can ship a real app."
  Part VII  From Language to Interfaces
  Part VIII Thinking in React
  Part IX   React + TypeScript
  Part X    Building Real Applications
  Part XI   Testing
  Part XII  Production-Ready React

BOOK THREE — MASTERY                                   "I can lead, design, and scale."
  Part XIII Advanced TypeScript
  Part XIV  Advanced React + TypeScript Patterns
  Part XV   Professional TypeScript & React Engineering
  Part XVI  Capstone

    16 parts · 99 chapters · 16 checkpoints · 20 projects · 3 capstone tracks.

    Why three Books?

    • Book One + Book Two = the Essential core. A reader who finishes them is a productive, job-ready TypeScript + React developer.
    • Book Three = mastery. It is valuable, and parts of it are mandatory for senior roles, but none of it is a prerequisite for being productive. This is how the book keeps specialist knowledge from feeling mandatory.

    1.5 The storyline that runs through the book

    A book feels cohesive when the reader keeps meeting the same problems at higher levels of sophistication. Five threads run from the first part to the last:

    Thread First appearance Matures in Final form
    Compile time vs runtime Ch 3: type erasure Ch 32: runtime safety Ch 61: "what TypeScript believes vs what the server returned" · Ch 96: server/client serialization boundary
    Make illegal states unrepresentable Ch 13: discriminated unions Ch 52 & 55: UI state and reducers Ch 90: domain modeling at scale
    Single source of truth for types Ch 20: typeof, as const Ch 32: types inferred from schemas Ch 94: shared contract packages in a monorepo
    Annotate boundaries, infer the rest Ch 6: inference Ch 50: component props as boundaries Ch 91: public API design
    Abstraction has a cost Ch 19: over-generic code Ch 89: choosing component patterns Ch 97: avoiding unnecessary abstraction in code review

    There is also a running project thread. TaskFlow (a task manager) starts as a typed data model in Part II, becomes a Node API in Part VI, a painful vanilla DOM app in Part VII, a React app in Part VIII, and a full React + API application with auth, forms, and tests in Parts X–XI. The reader watches the same domain improve as their skills grow, and the contrast between versions is the lesson.

    1.6 What makes this book different

    1. Problem before solution, always. No feature is introduced until the reader has felt the pain it removes.
    2. Mental models over memorization. One unifying model, types are sets of values, explains assignability, unions, intersections, never, unknown, generics constraints, and conditional types. React gets the same treatment: UI is a function of state and each render is a snapshot.
    3. Use it, then open the box. Utility types are used (Ch 21) before they are rebuilt with mapped and conditional types (Ch 22–23). Hooks are used before being framed by a mental model (Ch 43).
    4. Explicit "when NOT to use this". Every advanced pattern comes with its complexity cost.
    5. Runtime honesty. The book never lets the reader believe that a type annotation validates data.
    6. Practice everywhere. Four-level exercises in every chapter, projects in every part, a checkpoint after every part.
    7. Modern by default. strict mode from day one, ES modules, Vite, Vitest, React 19 idioms (ref as a prop, Actions), schema-first validation, and type-aware linting. Legacy patterns (forwardRef, defaultProps, CommonJS) are taught as things you will encounter, not things to write.

    1.7 Tooling baseline

    Concepts are tool-agnostic, but examples need concrete tools. Each choice below is the mainstream default at the time of writing. Every choice is explained in the book, and alternatives are named so the reader is never locked in.

    Concern Book default Alternatives named
    Language TypeScript (latest stable, strict: true) —
    Running TS directly tsx, Node's built-in type stripping ts-node, Bun, Deno
    Frontend build Vite (react-ts template) Next.js, React Router framework mode (Ch 96)
    UI library React 19 —
    Testing Vitest, React Testing Library, user-event, MSW, Playwright Jest, Cypress
    Linting / formatting ESLint (flat config) + typescript-eslint, Prettier Biome
    Runtime validation Zod (via the Standard Schema idea) Valibot, ArkType
    Server state TanStack Query SWR, RTK Query
    Client state Context + reducers, then Zustand Redux Toolkit, Jotai
    Routing React Router TanStack Router (type-safe routing sidebar)
    Forms Hand-built first, then React Hook Form, plus React 19 Actions TanStack Form
    Backend Node.js + Express (its any-typed req.body makes the boundary lesson vivid) Fastify, Hono
    Database SQLite + a TypeScript-first query layer (Drizzle) Prisma, Kysely
    Monorepo pnpm workspaces + project references Turborepo, Nx

    Version policy. The book teaches concepts that survive versions and isolates version-specific details in clearly marked "🆕 Modern note" and "🕰 Legacy note" sidebars, so it can be updated without rewriting chapters.

    1.8 Definition of done for the reader

    The reader has finished the journey when they can take a vague product requirement and:

    1. model the domain in types,
    2. design the API contract and validate it at runtime,
    3. build the backend and frontend with clear layer boundaries,
    4. handle every UI state (loading, empty, error, success, partial),
    5. test it at the right levels,
    6. ship it with production concerns addressed,
    7. explain every design decision, including the abstractions they chose not to build.

    That is exactly what the capstone asks them to do.

    2.1 The learning loop

    Every part of the book, and most chapters, moves through the same loop:

     ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │  1. FEEL THE PROBLEM      "This code breaks / repeats / lies to me."     │
 │  2. WHY A SOLUTION EXISTS "Someone hit this before; here's their answer."│
 │  3. LEARN THE CONCEPT     The idea in plain language first.              │
 │  4. BUILD A MENTAL MODEL  One picture that predicts behavior.            │
 │  5. TINY EXAMPLES         3–10 lines, one idea each.                     │
 │  6. PRACTICE              Level 1–2 exercises.                           │
 │  7. COMBINE               Mix with earlier concepts.                     │
 │  8. BUILD SOMETHING       Mini-project or project milestone.             │
 │  9. HIT REAL-WORLD WALLS  The simple solution stops being enough.        │
 │ 10. ADVANCED SOLUTION     The next chapter or part answers that wall.    │
 │ 11. PRODUCTION QUALITY    Tests, errors, edge cases, maintainability.    │
 └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                 ↑                                              │
                 └──────── step 9 of one chapter is ────────────┘
                           step 1 of a later one

    The last arrow is what makes it a book rather than a collection of pages: the walls hit at step 9 become the opening problems of later chapters.

    2.2 The eight questions

    Every important concept answers these eight questions somewhere in its chapter. Authors use them as a checklist, and readers use them as a self-test.

    # Question Where it is usually answered
    1 What is this? "The core idea"
    2 Why does it exist? Opening problem
    3 What problem does it solve? "A problem without X"
    4 How does it work? Mental model + "under the hood"
    5 When should I use it? "Use when" box
    6 When should I NOT use it? "🚫 When not to" box
    7 How does it connect to what I know? "🔗 Connections" box
    8 How is it used in real applications? "🌍 Real world" section

    2.3 Teaching principles

    1. Problem first. No syntax appears before the reader has seen code that fails, repeats itself, or silently lies.
    2. One unifying mental model per domain.
      • TypeScript: types are sets of values; assignability is "fits inside"; the compiler is a static, pessimistic reader of your code.
      • React: UI = f(state); every render is a snapshot; effects synchronize with things outside React.
      • Architecture: boundaries are where trust changes; types document boundaries, and validation enforces them.
    3. Spiral, don't dump. Big ideas are introduced lightly, used, then revisited in depth. unknown appears in Ch 9, returns in Ch 14 (narrowing), becomes central in Ch 32 (runtime safety), and is applied in Ch 61 (API data).
    4. Use it, then open the box. Readers use utility types before building them, and use useState before seeing the hooks mental model. Mastery comes from rebuilding what you already use.
    5. Concrete → abstract → concrete. Start from a specific example, extract the general rule, and immediately apply the rule to a new specific case.
    6. Inference first, annotation at boundaries. The book teaches the professional habit from Chapter 6 onward: let TypeScript infer locals; annotate function parameters, public APIs, and module boundaries.
    7. Honest about limits. Every chapter that adds power also says what it cannot do. Types do not validate data, memoization is not free, and abstraction has a cost.
    8. Manage cognitive load. Each chapter has one big idea. Prerequisites are named at the top. Specialist material is fenced off in clearly labeled ⏭ Safe to skip boxes.
    9. Retrieval over re-reading. Exercises ask readers to produce answers (predict the type, fix the error, design the API), not recognize them.
    10. Every part ends in something real. A project or project milestone closes every part.

    2.4 Chapter anatomy

    The book uses five chapter archetypes. A chapter is shaped by what it teaches; it is not forced into one template.

    A. Concept chapter (most chapters)

    The full anatomy. Steps can merge or be skipped when a concept is small.

     1. Why this problem exists          — the situation that creates the need
 2. A problem without <concept>      — real code that breaks, repeats, or lies
 3. The core idea                    — one paragraph, no syntax yet
 4. Mental model                     — a picture/analogy that predicts behavior
 5. First example                    — the smallest possible working version
 6. Syntax                           — only now, annotated piece by piece
 7. Step-by-step examples            — tiny → larger → realistic
 8. Common mistakes                  — with the actual compiler error and the fix
 9. When to use it
10. When NOT to use it               — simpler alternatives, complexity cost
11. Connections                      — backward links (and forward teasers)
12. Real-world example               — how it looks in a production codebase
13. Practice exercises               — Level 1 and Level 2
14. Challenge                        — Level 3 and Level 4
15. Chapter summary
16. Key takeaways                    — 3–7 sentences worth remembering
17. What comes next                  — the wall this chapter leaves you facing

    B. Story chapter (Ch 1, 2, 36)

    Hook (a scene or a bug) → Narrative (how we got here) → Demonstrations (small code that shows the pain)
→ The idea that changed things → What this means for you → Reflection questions

    C. Tooling chapter (Ch 5, 26, 27, 70, 76)

    A scenario that goes wrong → What the tool/setting actually changes (before/after output)
→ Recommended defaults and why → How to diagnose problems → "Break it and fix it" exercises

    Tooling chapters are deliberately not reference manuals. Each setting is taught by showing what changes in the output or the errors when you flip it.

    D. Pattern chapter (Part XIV, Ch 19, Ch 89)

    Real code with a recurring pain → The naive fix and why it decays → The pattern
→ Typed implementation (tiny → production) → ✅ When this is useful
→ 🚫 When this is unnecessary complexity → Refactoring exercise (apply it, then remove it)

    Every pattern chapter includes a "de-abstraction" exercise: the reader takes an over-engineered version and simplifies it. Knowing when not to use a pattern is a skill the book practices, not merely mentions.

    E. Integration / project chapter (Ch 19, 98, 99 and every project brief)

    Brief → Concepts used → Requirements → Suggested architecture → Milestones
→ Review checklist → Stretch goals → Reflection: "What should you understand now?"

    2.5 Recurring callouts

    Callouts are used consistently across the book so readers learn to scan for them:

    Callout Meaning
    🧠 Mental model The picture to keep in your head
    ⚠️ Common mistake Shown with the real error message and the fix
    🚫 When not to Simpler alternatives and the complexity cost
    🔗 Connection Links to earlier or later chapters
    🌍 Real world How this appears in production codebases and libraries
    🔬 Under the hood Optional deeper explanation; never required later
    ⏭ Safe to skip Specialist material you can postpone without penalty
    🆕 Modern note Recent language, library, or tooling behavior
    🕰 Legacy note Older patterns you will meet in existing code (e.g., forwardRef, CommonJS)
    🧪 Try it A 2-minute experiment in the editor or playground

    2.6 Explanation style guide

    Voice: an experienced engineer sitting next to the reader. Second person, direct, warm, never condescending. Opinions are labeled as opinions ("Many teams prefer…", "This book recommends…, because…").

    Do:

    • Intuition before syntax. Explain what a mapped type does ("loop over the keys and transform each property") before showing [K in keyof T].
    • Analogies, used sparingly and then retired. For example, generics are "function parameters for types", and an effect is "a subscription you must be able to cancel". Each analogy is followed by where it breaks down.
    • Visual explanations. Set diagrams for unions and intersections, render timelines for React, boundary diagrams for runtime validation, and dependency graphs for architecture.
    • Show the compiler's view. Use hover-type annotations in comments (// ^? string | undefined) so readers see what TypeScript infers.
    • Before/after and refactoring. Many lessons start from working-but-poor code and refactor it step by step, so the reader learns to improve code, not just write it.
    • Read real error messages. Errors are quoted verbatim and decoded. Reading TypeScript errors is taught as a skill (Ch 5) and practiced throughout.

    Avoid:

    • unexplained jargon (every term is defined at first use and collected in the glossary),
    • code dumps (no listing over ~40 lines in a lesson; larger code lives in examples/ and is walked through in pieces),
    • feature-list teaching ("TypeScript also has X, Y, and Z…"),
    • premature generality (no generic, overload, or pattern before the reader has written the concrete version),
    • "it just works" magic (every inference result is explained or explicitly deferred with a forward reference).

    2.7 Code example progression

    Every concept climbs the same four-rung ladder. A reader should never meet a rung before the rung below it.

    Rung Size Purpose Lives in
    1. Tiny 3–10 lines Isolate exactly one idea Inline in the lesson
    2. Slightly larger 10–30 lines Combine with one earlier idea Inline + examples/
    3. Realistic 30–80 lines Recognizable app code (a service, a hook, a component) examples/, walked through
    4. Production-style Multi-file Errors, edge cases, tests, naming, folder placement Projects, or the "🌍 Real world" section

    2.8 Exercise design

    Every major chapter ends with exercises at four levels:

    Level Name What it demands Guidance Typical time
    L1 Recall Apply the concept directly Fully specified, often "predict the type" or "fix the error" 5–10 min
    L2 Application Combine with earlier concepts Specified outcome, open method 15–30 min
    L3 Challenge Solve a less-guided problem Goal only; hints hidden behind a fold 30–90 min
    L4 Real-world Realistic development task A ticket-style brief with acceptance criteria 1–3 h

    Exercise formats used across the book: predict-the-type, fix-the-error, refactor-this, design-the-API, write-the-test-first, review-this-PR (spot the type smells), break-it (make the compiler complain on purpose), and remove-the-abstraction.

    Solutions policy. Solutions are not placed next to exercises. Each exercise folder contains starter/ and tests/ (auto-checking where possible, including type tests). Solutions live in a separate solutions/ tree, revealed per chapter, with a "try for 20 more minutes first" note. The reader is told explicitly: struggle is the point.

    2.9 Exemplar: Chapter 16 — "Why Generics?" fully blueprinted

    This is how one concept chapter looks when every step of the anatomy is filled in. It is the reference blueprint for authors.

    1. Why this problem exists. You've written utilities that work on "any kind of list". JavaScript doesn't care what's in the array, but TypeScript needs to know what comes out, based on what went in.

    2. A problem without generics.

    function firstString(items: string[]): string | undefined { return items[0]; }
function firstNumber(items: number[]): number | undefined { return items[0]; }
// …firstUser, firstTask, firstInvoice. Copy-paste forever, or:

function first(items: any[]): any { return items[0]; }
const n = first([1, 2, 3]);
n.toUpperCase(); // ✅ compiles, 💥 crashes: `any` erased everything we knew

    3. The core idea. Let the caller's type flow through the function. Write the function once, with a placeholder for "whatever type the items are".

    4. Mental model. 🧠 A type parameter is a function parameter for types. first(items) takes a value; first<T> also takes a type, and TypeScript usually fills it in for you by looking at the argument. (Where the analogy breaks: type parameters vanish at runtime. You cannot if (T === string).)

    5. First example.

    function first<T>(items: T[]): T | undefined {
  return items[0];
}
const n = first([1, 2, 3]);    // n: number | undefined
const s = first(["a", "b"]);   // s: string | undefined

    6. Syntax. <T> declares the parameter; items: T[] uses it to capture the input; T | undefined uses it again to describe the output. The golden rule, previewed here: a type parameter earns its place by appearing at least twice, because it exists to connect things.

    7. Step-by-step examples. last<T> → pair<A, B> → wrapInArray<T> → groupBy<T, K>, compared against the built-in Object.groupBy, which has the same shape.

    8. Common mistakes.

    • A type parameter used once: function log<T>(x: T): void (just use unknown).
    • Passing explicit type arguments everywhere (first<number>([1,2])) instead of trusting inference.
    • The lying generic: async function fetchJson<T>(url: string): Promise<T>. T appears only in the output, so it is a type assertion in disguise. Foreshadows Chapter 32.

    9. When to use it. When the output type depends on the input type, or when two parameters must agree ((items: T[], predicate: (item: T) => boolean)).

    10. When NOT to use it. When every caller uses the same type, when a union says it better (string | number), or when unknown is honest enough.

    11. Connections. 🔗 You've already used generics: Array<T> (Ch 7), Promise<T> (Ch 11), Map<K, V>. Next: constraints (Ch 17). Later: useState<T> (Ch 52), generic components (Ch 57).

    12. Real-world example. A data-loading helper evolving to production style:

    // Realistic, but it lies: T is never checked.
async function fetchJson<T>(url: string): Promise<T> {
  const res = await fetch(url);
  return res.json();
}

// Production-style: T is *inferred from a parser*, so the type is earned.
async function fetchJson<T>(url: string, parse: (data: unknown) => T): Promise<T> {
  const res = await fetch(url);
  if (!res.ok) throw new HttpError(res.status, url);
  return parse(await res.json());
}
const user = await fetchJson("/api/me", (data) => UserSchema.parse(data)); // user: User

    13. Practice (L1, L2). Predict the inferred type of five calls. Convert three duplicated functions into one generic function.

    14. Challenge (L3, L4). L3: write zip<A, B>. L4: a ticket asking for a typed retry<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>, attempts: number): Promise<T> used by the TaskFlow API client.

    15–16. Summary & takeaways. Generics preserve information that any destroys. Inference does most of the work. A type parameter must connect at least two places. A generic that appears only in a return type is an unchecked assertion.

    17. What comes next. "Our getProperty(obj, key) accepts any key, even ones that don't exist. How do we tell TypeScript that key must belong to obj?" → Chapter 17: constraints and keyof.

    Section 3Why JavaScript → TypeScript → React

    This section is written in the book's own voice. It is the narrative spine of Part I (Ch 1–3) and Ch 36 (Why React?), condensed. Each beat of the story maps to the chapter that teaches it (see §3.8).

    3.1 A language built in ten days for small jobs

    In May 1995, Brendan Eich at Netscape was given about ten days to build a scripting language for the browser. The goal was modest: let web designers add a bit of interactivity to a page, such as validating a form field, swapping an image on hover, or showing an alert.

    That goal shaped everything about JavaScript:

    • Forgiving. A typo shouldn't take down a page, so the language tries hard to keep going ("5" * 2 is 10, "5" + 2 is "52").
    • Dynamic. Variables have no declared types; any value can go anywhere.
    • Small programs, single authors. A script was a few dozen lines, written and read by one person, usually in one sitting.

    For that job, dynamic typing is a feature. When the whole program fits on one screen, the author is the type checker.

    3.2 JavaScript escapes the small job

    Then the web changed, and JavaScript was asked to do far more than it was designed for:

    1995  JavaScript ships in Netscape Navigator: form checks, hover effects
1997  Standardized as ECMAScript
2004  Gmail: a full application living in a browser tab
2005  "Ajax" gets a name; Google Maps makes the web feel like a desktop
2006  jQuery tames the browser DOM
2008  Chrome's V8 engine makes JavaScript *fast*
2008  ECMAScript 4, which proposed optional static types, is abandoned
2009  Node.js: JavaScript on the server, one language everywhere
2010  npm: an explosion of shared packages
2015  ES2015: modules, classes, arrow functions, promises

    By the 2010s, codebases had grown from 50 lines to 500,000. Teams grew from one author to hundreds. The assumptions that made dynamic typing comfortable broke one by one.

    3.3 What breaks when JavaScript gets big

    None of these problems are dramatic on their own. Together, at scale, they are expensive.

    1. Errors arrive late, at runtime, in front of users.

    function shippingLabel(order) {
  return `${order.customer.adress.city}, ${order.customer.address.zip}`;
  //                         ^^^^^^ typo: nothing complains until this line runs
}
// TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'city')

    2. Wrong values flow silently.

    function addTax(price, rate) { return price + price * rate; }
addTax(input.value, 0.2); // input.value is the string "100"
// "100" + 20 → "10020" — no crash, just a wrong invoice

    3. Refactoring becomes risky. Rename user.name to user.fullName in a 300-file codebase. Search-and-replace finds name in a thousand unrelated places. Miss one usage, and you ship undefined to production.

    4. APIs are undiscoverable. What does this function accept?

    createChart(container, data, options); // Which options exist? Is `data` an array? Of what?

    The answer lives in someone's head, an outdated wiki, or the source code three folders away.

    5. Teams can't hold the whole program in their heads. Every function call is a contract between two people who may never meet. In JavaScript, those contracts are invisible.

    6. null and undefined are everywhere.

    document.querySelector("#save").addEventListener("click", save);
// Works today. Someone renames the button's id, and the page breaks.
// TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'addEventListener')

    Large companies responded in different ways. Google annotated JavaScript with types in comments (Closure Compiler), Facebook built Flow, and others moved to languages that compiled to JavaScript (CoffeeScript, Dart). The industry was asking for one thing: static analysis, meaning tools that read your code before it runs and tell you what will go wrong.

    3.4 TypeScript: JavaScript, plus a second opinion before runtime

    In October 2012, Microsoft announced TypeScript, led by Anders Hejlsberg (the designer of Turbo Pascal, Delphi, and C#). Microsoft had the same pain as everyone else: its own teams were building large browser applications in JavaScript and finding them hard to scale and maintain.

    The key design decision was humility: TypeScript would not replace JavaScript. It would describe it.

    • A superset. Every JavaScript program is (syntactically) a TypeScript program. You can adopt TypeScript one file at a time.
    • Types are erased. The output is plain JavaScript. TypeScript adds no runtime and no new semantics; it only checks.
    • Follows the standard. New JavaScript features come from the ECMAScript committee; TypeScript types them.
    • Pragmatic, not academically pure. The type system is deliberately not fully sound. It trades some theoretical guarantees for working well with real JavaScript.
    function addTax(price: number, rate: number): number {
  return price + price * rate;
}
addTax(input.value, 0.2);
//     ~~~~~~~~~~~ Argument of type 'string' is not assignable to parameter of type 'number'.

    The bug from §3.3 is now caught in the editor, before the code ever runs, at the moment it was written. That timing is the whole value proposition.

    The second gift: the editor knows your code

    Types don't just catch errors. They power autocomplete, go-to-definition, safe automated renames, inline documentation, and "find all references". For many teams, refactoring confidence and discoverability turned out to be worth more than bug-catching.

    Adoption

    TypeScript 1.0 shipped in 2014. Angular 2 (2016) was written in TypeScript, and strictNullChecks (TypeScript 2.0) attacked the null problem directly. Through the late 2010s, editors, frameworks, and library authors standardized on it. By 2025, GitHub reported TypeScript as its most-used language by contributors, and new tooling pushed further: Node.js can now run TypeScript files directly by stripping their types, and the compiler itself is being ported to native code for much faster type-checking.

    3.5 The boundary every TypeScript developer must understand

    Here is the most important idea in this book's first part:

    // What you write                      // What runs (types erased)
function greet(name: string) {         function greet(name) {
  return `Hello, ${name}`;               return `Hello, ${name}`;
}                                      }

    Types exist at compile time only. At runtime, there are no types left to check anything. So:

    type User = { id: string; email: string };

const user = (await response.json()) as User;
//     TypeScript *believes* this is a User. The server may disagree.
user.email.toLowerCase(); // 💥 if the server sent { id: 1, mail: "…" }

    TypeScript checks your code's internal consistency. It cannot check the outside world: network responses, localStorage, environment variables, user input, or third-party JavaScript. That is why JavaScript knowledge remains fundamental, and why the book returns to runtime validation again and again (Ch 32, 61, 64, 96).

    Research on public JavaScript projects has estimated that static type checkers would have caught roughly 15% of shipped bugs. That is significant, but it is not everything. The rest is the job of tests, validation, and design. (Ch 66 builds this layered safety model.)

    3.6 Meanwhile, in the browser: UIs became state machines

    While TypeScript tackled the language problem, front-end developers had a different crisis: keeping the screen in sync with the data.

    The jQuery-era approach was imperative: when something changes, find the right DOM nodes and patch them.

    // Mark a task done. Also update the counter, the empty state, the filter tabs, the title…
checkbox.addEventListener("change", () => {
  task.done = checkbox.checked;
  row.classList.toggle("done", task.done);
  counter.textContent = `${tasks.filter((t) => !t.done).length} left`;
  emptyState.hidden = tasks.length > 0;
  // …and every other place that displays tasks. Forget one, and the UI lies.
});

    Every new feature multiplies the update paths. With n pieces of state and m places that display them, you maintain up to n × m manual synchronizations. Facebook lived this at enormous scale; its notification and chat counters were famously hard to keep consistent.

    In 2013, Facebook open-sourced React, created by Jordan Walke, with a radical idea:

    Don't update the UI. Describe it. UI = f(state). When state changes, call the function again; React works out what changed in the DOM.

    function TaskSummary({ tasks }) {
  const left = tasks.filter((t) => !t.done).length;
  return tasks.length === 0 ? <EmptyState /> : <p>{left} left</p>;
}

    There are no manual updates and no forgotten paths: one description, re-run whenever state changes. Add components (UI pieces you compose like functions), props (inputs), state (memory), and later hooks (2019), and React became the most widely used way to build interfaces, including on mobile via React Native.

    3.7 Why TypeScript + React is the combination

    React made UIs composable functions of data. TypeScript made functions and data describable and checkable. Together:

    React concept What TypeScript adds
    A component is a function Its props are a typed contract: misuse is an editor error, not a blank screen
    Props flow down a tree Renaming a prop updates or flags every usage across the app
    UI state has shapes (loading, error, success…) Discriminated unions make impossible UI states unrepresentable
    Events carry data Typed events: no more guessing what e.target is
    Context and hooks share logic Typed hooks make shared logic self-documenting
    Data comes from APIs Types + runtime validation define safe boundaries
    Component libraries serve many teams Types are the documentation that never goes stale

    Today, the default React starters (Vite's react-ts template, Next.js, React Router) start in TypeScript. TypeScript + React is no longer an upgrade path; it is the baseline.

    Section 4Complete Learning Roadmap

    The roadmap is about learning progression: what a learner must be able to do, in what order. The book (Section 11) is about teaching that progression. The two correspond closely but not one-to-one.

    This section shows the first-draft roadmap, a critical review of it, and the final roadmap that the book is built on.

    4.1 Roadmap v1 (first draft, following the brief's suggested order)

    Why TypeScript → JS checkpoint → TS fundamentals → type system → functions → objects & interfaces
→ unions & narrowing → classes → generics → type manipulation → utility types → modules & config
→ declarations → JS interop → Node.js → runtime safety → ADVANCED TS → PROFESSIONAL TS
→ Why React → React fundamentals → hooks → React + TS → ADVANCED REACT + TS → architecture
→ API integration → forms → testing → production → professional React → capstone

    4.2 Critical review of v1

    # Problem found Why it hurts learning Fix applied in v2
    1 Advanced and Professional TypeScript come before any UI work Creates a motivation cliff: weeks of type-level programming before building anything visible. Variance and branded types are abstract until you've felt the bugs they prevent, and publishing a library is meaningless with nothing to publish. Moved to Book Three (after real apps). A TypeScript-first reading path (§4.6) still lets backend-minded readers go straight there.
    2 Utility types come after mapped/conditional types Backwards for learners. Partial<T> is useful on day one; requiring mapped types first delays a practical tool for an abstract one. Use, then open the box: Deriving types (Ch 20) → using utility types (Ch 21) → mapped types rebuild Partial/Pick (Ch 22) → conditional types rebuild Exclude/ReturnType (Ch 23) → custom utilities (Ch 24).
    3 Testing only appears near the end Teaches "testing is an afterthought". Every project before it is untested. Testing starts in Part IV. The starter repo from Ch 5 ships with Vitest preconfigured, and Ch 19 teaches testing generic code (runtime tests + type tests). Ch 27 explains and extends the toolchain. Every project from P04 onward ships with tests, and Part XI deepens testing for React.
    4 "Why React?" is told, not felt Readers who never fought manual DOM synchronization don't appreciate declarative UI. New bridge part: typing the DOM (Ch 35) and building Vanilla TaskFlow (P09). The pain becomes the motivation for Ch 36. This also previews DOM and event types that React uses.
    5 Advanced React patterns come before building a real app Compound and polymorphic components solve library-scale duplication the learner hasn't met yet, so they become premature abstraction. Real apps → testing → production first. Advanced patterns move to Part XIV. Generic components essentials stay in core (Ch 57) because forms and data features need them.
    6 Runtime safety is a single late stop The compile-time/runtime boundary is the most misunderstood idea, and one chapter is not enough. It becomes a spiral thread: erasure (Ch 3) → unknown (Ch 9) → narrowing (Ch 14) → runtime safety (Ch 32) → API data (Ch 61) → forms (Ch 64) → server/client boundary (Ch 96).
    7 Hooks are a list of APIs Learners memorize hooks without knowing which problem each solves. State first (Ch 41), then a hooks mental model (Ch 43) that frames each hook as the answer to a question.
    8 Missing real-world skills Reading compiler errors, DOM typing, enums vs unions, error-handling design, routing, server state vs client state, accessibility, security, observability, E2E testing, styling, and frameworks/Server Components are all absent or implicit. Each now has a home: Ch 5, 35, 8, 33, 59, 60/62, 73, 74, 75, 69, 58/93, 96.
    9 Config is taught late, but needed from day one Readers would run code with settings they don't understand. Ch 5 gives a starter config with explicit "explained in Ch 26" forward references. Strict mode is on from the first program.
    10 Professional TS and Professional React overlap Architecture, documentation, and team practices would be taught twice. Merged into one Professional Engineering part (Part XV), organized by concern rather than by technology.
    11 Projects cluster at the end Long stretches without building anything. At least one project per part, plus the running TaskFlow thread that evolves across six parts.
    12 Duplicate concept risk: props, state, reducers React fundamentals and React + TS would both "teach props". Clear split: Part VIII teaches what props/state are (concept, light types); Part IX teaches how to design their types (contracts). useReducer is taught once, in Ch 55, where discriminated unions make it shine.

    4.3 Roadmap v2 (final)

    The final roadmap has 13 stages grouped into three phases.

PHASE 2 · INTERFACES & APPLICATIONS ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
