    🧵 TaskFlow thread: P02 (domain model) → P07 (API) → P08 (client) → P09 (vanilla UI) → P11 (React) → P14 (full app) → P15 (auth) → P16 (tests). One domain, six levels of sophistication.

    6.2 Project specifications

    P01 — Typed Calculator

    • Difficulty: 🟢 Beginner · When: end of Part II · Prerequisites: Ch 5–9
    • Concepts used: primitives, annotations vs inference, literal unions (Operator), tuples, functions, unknown for raw input, null/undefined handling.
    • Requirements:
      1. A terminal REPL that evaluates a <op> b for + - * / % **.
      2. Rejects invalid input with a helpful message (never crashes).
      3. Handles division by zero explicitly (no Infinity shown to the user).
      4. Keeps a history of the last 10 results and supports history and clear.
      5. Memory commands: M+, M-, MR, MC.
    • Suggested architecture:
      p01-typed-calculator/
  src/parse.ts      # string → { left, operator, right } | ParseError
  src/evaluate.ts   # pure arithmetic, no I/O
  src/memory.ts     # history + memory state
  src/cli.ts        # the only file that touches stdin/stdout (a boundary!)
    • Stretch goals: operator precedence and parentheses (a recursive-descent parser); a bigint mode; return later to add Vitest tests (after Ch 19).
    • You should understand afterward: annotate boundaries and infer locals; literal unions as a vocabulary; raw input is untrusted text, the first glimpse of "boundaries".

    P02 — TaskFlow Core (typed todo domain)

    • Difficulty: 🟢 Beginner · When: Part III, after Ch 14 (extended after Ch 15) · Prerequisites: Ch 8, 10–14
    • Concepts used: interfaces and aliases, discriminated unions for the task lifecycle, narrowing, exhaustiveness, readonly data, option objects, custom errors (Ch 15).
    • Requirements:
      1. Create, edit, complete, reopen, and archive tasks; tasks belong to projects.
      2. The lifecycle is modeled as a discriminated union: an archived task cannot be completed, and a blocked task must have a reason. The type system enforces this, not runtime ifs alone.
      3. Filter by status, priority, tag, and due date; compute "overdue".
      4. Pure domain functions (completeTask(task): DoneTask) return new objects; no mutation.
      5. Save to and load from a JSON file; loading treats the file content as unknown.
    • Suggested architecture:
      p02-taskflow-core/
  src/domain/task.ts        # types + pure transition functions
  src/domain/project.ts
  src/domain/filters.ts
  src/store/task-store.ts   # in-memory collection
  src/persistence/file.ts   # boundary: JSON in/out
  src/cli.ts
    • Stretch goals: an undo stack; recurring tasks; a TaskRepository interface with an InMemoryTaskRepository class (Ch 15).
    • You should understand afterward: how to make illegal states unrepresentable; why domain logic is pure and separate from I/O. This core is reused in P07 and P11.

    P03 — Utility Toolkit

    • Difficulty: 🟢 Beginner · When: Part III, after Ch 11 · Prerequisites: Ch 11
    • Concepts used: parameter/return types, optional/default/rest parameters, callbacks, higher-order functions, overloads, async functions.
    • Requirements:
      1. String helpers: slugify, truncate, capitalize, formatCurrency(amount, options?).
      2. Function helpers: debounce, throttle, once.
      3. Async helpers: sleep, withTimeout, retry.
      4. Array helpers written for specific types only (chunkNumbers, uniqueStrings, firstTask). This is deliberate.
      5. A README documenting each function's contract.
    • Suggested architecture: src/string.ts, src/function.ts, src/async.ts, src/array.ts, src/index.ts.
    • Stretch goals: overloads for formatDate(date) vs formatDate(date, pattern); cancellable debounce.
    • You should understand afterward: function contracts, and the pain of type-specific duplication, which Chapter 16 resolves. The reader should feel the need for generics before learning them.

    P04 — Generic Utility Library

    • Difficulty: 🟡 Intermediate · When: Part IV, Ch 19 (tooling added in Ch 27) · Prerequisites: Ch 16–19 (and P03)
    • Concepts used: generic functions, constraints, keyof, indexed access, generic types (Result<T, E>), inference-first design, runtime tests and type tests.
    • Requirements:
      1. Make P03's array helpers generic: chunk<T>, unique<T>, uniqueBy<T, K>, groupBy<T, K>, partition<T>, sortBy<T, K extends keyof T>, pick, omit.
      2. Generic async helpers: retry<T>, withTimeout<T>, pLimit (concurrency limit).
      3. Result<T, E> with ok, err, map, mapError, unwrapOr.
      4. Every function has runtime tests and type tests; no explicit type arguments are needed at any call site in the tests.
      5. Published locally as a package consumed by later projects (with .d.ts output after Ch 28).
    • Suggested architecture:
      p04-generic-utils/
  src/array/   src/object/   src/async/   src/result/
  src/index.ts                 # explicit public API
  test/*.test.ts  test/*.test-d.ts (type tests)
    • Stretch goals: a typed pipe up to 8 functions; debounce that preserves parameter types via generics; benchmark groupBy against Object.groupBy.
    • You should understand afterward: inference-first API design, the golden rule of generics, and testing types as specifications.

    P05 — Type-Safe Event Emitter

    • Difficulty: 🟠 Advanced · When: end of Part IV · Prerequisites: Ch 16–24
    • Concepts used: generic constraints with keyof, indexed access, mapped types, template literal types, function types, type tests.
    • Requirements:
      1. createEmitter<Events>() where Events maps event names to payload types, e.g. { "task:created": Task; "task:deleted": { id: string } }.
      2. on, off, once, and emit are fully typed: wrong event names and wrong payloads are compile errors.
      3. on returns an unsubscribe function.
      4. One failing listener doesn't stop the others; errors are reported to an onError hook.
      5. Type tests prove that misuse fails to compile (@ts-expect-error).
    • Suggested architecture: src/types.ts (EventMap, Listener<T>), src/emitter.ts, test/emitter.test.ts, test/emitter.test-d.ts.
    • Stretch goals: namespace wildcards (on("task:*", …) receives a union of all task: payloads, using template literal types); waitFor(event): Promise<Payload>; async listeners with emitAsync.
    • You should understand afterward: type-level key → value mapping, and how libraries achieve "autocomplete everything" APIs.

    P06 — Legacy JS → TS Migration

    • Difficulty: 🟡 Intermediate · When: Part V, Ch 29 · Prerequisites: Ch 25–29
    • Concepts used: allowJs, checkJs, JSDoc types, declaration files for untyped dependencies, ESM conversion, strict flags, any reduction, type coverage.
    • Provided: Shelfie, a ~3,000-line legacy Node + Express bookstore written in CommonJS with callbacks, a dynamic config blob, a mixin, a hand-rolled event bus, an untyped vendored library, and a passing test suite.
    • Requirements (one stage per pull request; tests must pass after every stage):
      1. Add TypeScript with allowJs; the build and tests pass with zero behavior change.
      2. Turn on checkJs and add JSDoc to the three core modules.
      3. Write a .d.ts for the vendored library.
      4. Convert leaf modules to .ts, then the core.
      5. Convert to ES Modules.
      6. Enable strict flags one at a time.
      7. Reduce explicit and implicit any below a target, measured by a type-coverage tool.
    • Suggested architecture: keep the original structure. Add MIGRATION.md with a per-stage log of errors fixed, any count, and decisions made.
    • Stretch goals: a CI gate that fails if type coverage drops; a small codemod for a repetitive conversion.
    • You should understand afterward: migration as a ratchet; risk management on a live codebase; how to measure type safety.

    P07 — TaskFlow API (Node.js)

    • Difficulty: 🟡 Intermediate · When: Part VI (v1 in Ch 31, v2 in Ch 32–33) · Prerequisites: Ch 30–33, P02
    • Concepts used: Node + TypeScript, Express, DTOs vs domain types, service and repository layers, SQLite, schema validation with inferred types, env validation, error contracts, tests.
    • Requirements:
      1. REST endpoints for projects and tasks: CRUD, filtering, sorting, and pagination.
      2. A lifecycle transition endpoint (POST /tasks/:id/transitions) that reuses P02's domain rules.
      3. Every request body, params object, and query string is parsed by a schema; failures return 400 with field-level errors.
      4. A consistent error contract ({ error: { code, message, details? } }), mapped exhaustively from domain errors.
      5. Validated environment config; the server refuses to start when it's misconfigured.
      6. Integration tests against a test database.
    • Suggested architecture:
      p07-taskflow-api/src/
  config/        # env schema → typed config
  domain/        # from P02 (pure)
  schemas/       # request/response schemas (types inferred)
  repositories/  # TaskRepository interface + sqlite + in-memory
  services/      # business rules, no HTTP
  http/          # routes, middleware, error mapping
  errors/        # domain error hierarchy
    • Stretch goals: an OpenAPI document generated from schemas; request IDs in logs; optimistic concurrency with a version field.
    • You should understand afterward: layered architecture with typed seams; DTO vs domain; "parse, don't validate"; error translation across layers. This API is the backend for Book Two.

    P08 — Typed API Client

    • Difficulty: 🟡 Intermediate · When: end of Part VI · Prerequisites: Ch 32–33, P04, P07
    • Concepts used: generics, fetch, schemas, Result<T, E>, discriminated error unions, AbortSignal, retries.
    • Requirements:
      1. createApiClient({ baseUrl, fetch? }) exposes typed methods for every TaskFlow endpoint.
      2. Every response is validated, so server drift becomes a typed validation error rather than a crash.
      3. Methods return Result<T, ApiError>, where ApiError is network | timeout | http | validation.
      4. Timeouts and cancellation through AbortSignal; retry with backoff for idempotent methods only.
      5. Works in both Node and the browser (no Node-only imports).
    • Suggested architecture: src/http.ts (one request function), src/endpoints/tasks.ts, src/endpoints/projects.ts, src/errors.ts, src/index.ts. Schemas are imported from the API's contract module.
    • Stretch goals: derive all methods from a single endpoint-definition object using mapped types; auth interceptors (needed in P15).
    • You should understand afterward: the client side of the boundary. Ch 61 builds React data fetching on top of this client.

    6.3 Checkpoints — Parts I–VI

    Each checkpoint has the same structure: Know · Build · Answer · Small challenge · Optional project · Ready signs · If you struggle, revisit.

    ✅ Checkpoint — Part I · Why TypeScript?

    • Know: why dynamic typing struggles at scale; what "superset" and "type erasure" mean; the compile-time/runtime split.
    • Build: nothing yet. You should be able to explain.
    • Answer:
      1. Name four problems large JavaScript codebases face and how types address each.
      2. What does tsc output for a file containing only interfaces?
      3. Why can't TypeScript guarantee that await res.json() is a User?
      4. What cannot TypeScript catch? Give three examples.
    • Small challenge: write a 10-line program that type-checks and still crashes. Explain why that is not a TypeScript bug.
    • Optional project: the L4 exercise from Ch 4 (a plain-JS fetch + DOM page).
    • Ready signs: you can explain erasure to a non-TypeScript developer in under a minute; the JavaScript checkpoint (Ch 4) scored ≥ 80%.
    • If you struggle, revisit: Ch 3 (erasure, boundaries); Ch 4 recommended JavaScript resources for any topic scoring below 2/3.

    ✅ Checkpoint — Part II · TypeScript Foundations

    • Know: annotations vs inference; primitives, arrays, tuples, object types, optional/readonly; aliases, interfaces, literal types; any vs unknown; void, never, null, undefined.
    • Build: P01 Typed Calculator.
    • Answer:
      1. When should you annotate, and when should you rely on inference?
      2. What's the difference between prop?: string and prop: string | undefined?
      3. Why is unknown safer than any?
      4. What does noUncheckedIndexedAccess change, and why does this book enable it?
      5. Why do many teams prefer literal unions over enums?
    • Small challenge: remove every any from a provided 60-line file without adding a single as.
    • Optional project: extend P01 with operator precedence.
    • Ready signs: you read a compiler error and know where to look; you rarely write redundant annotations.
    • If you struggle, revisit: Ch 5 §6 (reading errors), Ch 6 (inference), Ch 9 (edge types).

    ✅ Checkpoint — Part III · Thinking in Types

    • Know: types as sets; assignability; structural typing and excess property checks; typing functions, overloads, and this; interfaces vs aliases; unions and intersections; discriminated unions; every narrowing technique; type guards and assertion functions; exhaustiveness; classes and when not to use them.
    • Build: P02 TaskFlow Core and P03 Utility Toolkit.
    • Answer:
      1. Explain assignability using the set model, with an example in each direction.
      2. Why does an object literal with an extra property fail, when the same object in a variable passes?
      3. Turn { isLoading: boolean; error?: Error; data?: T } into a discriminated union and explain what bugs disappear.
      4. Why can narrowing be lost inside a callback?
      5. What's the difference between private and #private?
      6. When would you choose an interface over a type alias?
    • Small challenge: add a "cancelled" status to TaskFlow and let exhaustiveness errors guide you to every place that needs updating.
    • Optional project: model a vending machine's states and transitions.
    • Ready signs: your first instinct for "several possible states" is a discriminated union; you can predict narrowed types without hovering.
    • If you struggle, revisit: Ch 10 (set model), Ch 13 §5–6 (discriminated unions), Ch 14 §6–10 (narrowing and exhaustiveness).

    ✅ Checkpoint — Part IV · Generics & Type Transformations ⭐

    • Know: generic functions, types, interfaces, and classes; constraints; keyof; indexed access; generic defaults and inference; typeof, as const, satisfies; all built-in utility types; mapped types; conditional types; infer; distributivity; template literal types; custom utility types and their cost.
    • Build: P04 Generic Utility Library and P05 Type-Safe Event Emitter.
    • Answer:
      1. What is the golden rule of generics, and what is a "lying generic"?
      2. Explain <T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K] in plain English.
      3. When would you use satisfies instead of a type annotation?
      4. Implement Partial<T> and Exclude<T, U> from memory.
      5. Why does Exclude<"a" | "b", "a"> work "per member"?
      6. When should you not write a custom utility type?
    • Small challenge: write ValueOf<T> and PartialBy<T, K> with type tests, in 20 minutes.
    • Optional project: add namespace wildcards to P05.
    • Ready signs: call sites of your generic code never need explicit type arguments; you can read the type signature of a utility in a library's .d.ts.
    • If you struggle, revisit: Ch 16–17 (if generics feel magical), Ch 20 (if you duplicate types), Ch 22–23 (if utility types feel like black boxes). Do not skip this checkpoint. Parts IX, XIII, and XIV depend on it heavily.
    • Fast-track note: Ch 23–24 are Advanced tier. On reading path B you may skip them, along with questions 4 (the Exclude half), 5, and 6 and with P05, and return before Part XIII.

    ✅ Checkpoint — Part V · Toolchain & Ecosystem

    • Know: ESM vs CommonJS; type-only imports; module resolution modes; the purpose of each major tsconfig group; ESLint, Prettier, and Vitest roles; type tests; declaration files; @types; module augmentation; JS → TS migration strategy.
    • Build: P06 Legacy Migration (at least stages 1–4).
    • Answer:
      1. Why do single-file transpilers need isolatedModules / verbatimModuleSyntax?
      2. What's the difference between moduleResolution: "bundler" and "nodenext"?
      3. What does declare module "x" do, and when is it dangerous?
      4. Which tool should catch a floating promise, and why not tsc?
      5. Describe a safe order for enabling strict flags in a legacy codebase.
    • Small challenge: make a path alias that works in tsc, Vitest, and the runtime.
    • Optional project: finish P06 stages 5–7.
    • Ready signs: you can set up a new project from scratch without copying a config you don't understand.
    • If you struggle, revisit: Ch 25 (if import errors confuse you), Ch 26 (if config is copy-paste), Ch 28 (if .d.ts files feel mysterious).
    • Fast-track note: Ch 29 and P06 are Advanced tier. On reading path B, skip question 5 and P06, and return when you first join a mixed JS/TS codebase.

    ✅ Checkpoint — Part VI · Server & Boundaries

    • Know: Node + TypeScript setup; @types/node; env and file-system boundaries; layered API design; DTOs; repository and service patterns; database typing; unknown at boundaries; schema validation and inferred types; env validation; error design across layers.
    • Build: P07 TaskFlow API and P08 Typed API Client.
    • Answer:
      1. Explain "what TypeScript believes vs what the runtime receives" with an example from your API.
      2. List every boundary in P07 and how each is protected.
      3. Why are DTOs and domain types different types?
      4. When is a Result type better than throwing?
      5. Why validate responses from a service you control?
    • Small challenge: send ten malicious or malformed payloads to your API; every one should produce a clean 400 with no crash and no stack trace.
    • Optional project: generate OpenAPI docs from your schemas.
    • Ready signs: writing as SomeType on external data now feels wrong to you.
    • If you struggle, revisit: Ch 32 (all of it, as it is the most important chapter in Book One), Ch 31 §3–6 (layers), Ch 33 §1 and §5 (error translation).

    🎓 End of Book One. You can now think in types, design typed APIs, configure and test TypeScript projects, and protect runtime boundaries. Next: using all of it to build interfaces.

    Part VIIFrom Language to Interfaces

    Folder: 07-from-language-to-interfaces/ · Roadmap: Stage 5 — From Language to Interfaces · Difficulty: 🟡

    Purpose of the part. "You now understand the TypeScript language. Now let's use it to build interfaces." This part connects TypeScript to the browser, has the reader build a real UI without React, and turns the resulting pain into the motivation for React.

    Chapter 34The Bridge: TypeScript Concepts You'll Use in React

    Beginner Essential 34-the-bridge/

    Opens with: a 25-line React component shown on day one, with every TypeScript concept in it highlighted. Readers discover they already understand most of it. Mental model: React is "just" TypeScript: components are functions, props are parameter objects, hooks are generic functions, and UI states are unions.

    1. From language to interfaces — what changes when code produces UI instead of values.
    2. Functions become components — a component is a function from props to UI.
    3. Objects and destructuring become props — the parameter-object pattern you already know.
    4. Modules become component files — one concept per file, type-only imports for props types.
    5. Interfaces and aliases become contracts — props types as the component's public API.
    6. Unions and narrowing become UI states — conditional rendering is narrowing.
    7. Generics appear in hooks and components — useState<T>, useRef<T>, generic lists.
    8. Utility types shape props — Omit, Partial, Pick, and ComponentProps.
    9. Inference does the heavy lifting — useState(0) needs no annotation.
    10. Bridge self-check — a quiz mapping each TypeScript chapter to its React use.
    TypeScript concept Where it appears in React Chapter
    Functions, callbacks Components, event handlers, callback props 39, 41, 51
    Objects, destructuring Props, state objects 39, 50
    Modules, import type Component files, shared types 38, 58
    Interfaces / aliases Props contracts, context values 50, 54
    Unions, narrowing Conditional rendering, UI states, reducers 40, 52, 55
    Generics useState<T>, useRef<T>, custom hooks, generic components 52, 53, 56, 57
    Utility types ComponentProps, Omit for wrappers, Partial for updates 50, 52
    Inference Hooks, inline handlers (contextual typing) 51, 52

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Annotate a provided component, labeling every TypeScript concept it uses.
    • L2 Application: Rewrite a function-based "render to string" helper as a component-like function with typed props.
    • L3 Challenge: Predict the inferred types in a component that uses useState, map, and an inline handler.
    • L4 Real-world: Read a small open-source React + TS component and write a "what I recognize vs what's new" list.

    Chapter 35TypeScript in the Browser: Typing the DOM

    Intermediate Essential 35-typing-the-dom/

    Opens with: document.querySelector("#email").value gives Object is possibly 'null' and then Property 'value' does not exist on type 'Element'. Two errors in one line, and both are right. Mental model: 🧠 The DOM is a typed class hierarchy described by lib.dom.d.ts: EventTarget → Node → Element → HTMLElement → HTMLInputElement. Selecting an element only tells TypeScript the most general thing it can prove.

    1. lib.dom.d.ts — the browser described in types; the lib setting.
    2. The element hierarchy — reading the inheritance chain; tag-name maps.
    3. Selecting elements safely — querySelector with tag names vs selectors; instanceof checks vs as vs generic arguments.
    4. Typed DOM events — addEventListener inference via event maps; MouseEvent, KeyboardEvent, InputEvent, SubmitEvent.
    5. target vs currentTarget — why e.target is just EventTarget | null.
    6. Forms and inputs — string values, valueAsNumber, FormData.
    7. Browser APIs at the boundary — fetch, localStorage (string | null → JSON → unknown), URL parameters.
    8. Building Vanilla TaskFlow — rendering a list, adding, toggling, filtering, counting, with no framework.
    9. The pain log — recording every state/DOM synchronization bug you hit (this feeds Ch 36).

    Common mistakes: as HTMLInputElement everywhere · ignoring null from selectors · reading e.target.value without narrowing. Project: P09 Vanilla TaskFlow.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Give the type returned by six different querySelector calls.
    • L2 Application: Write getRequiredElement<T extends Element>(selector, ctor) that throws helpfully if missing.
    • L3 Challenge: Add keyboard navigation to the vanilla task list.
    • L4 Real-world: Add a "filter + counter + empty state" feature to P09 and log how many places needed manual updates.

    Chapter 36Why React?

    Beginner Essential 36-why-react/

    Archetype: Story chapter. Opens with: the reader's own pain log from P09: "Counter wrong after delete", "empty state shown with 2 items", "filter tab not highlighted after reload". Mental model: 🧠 UI = f(state). Stop writing instructions for changing the screen; write a description of what the screen should be for any given state, and let React work out the changes.

    1. Traditional DOM manipulation — imperative updates: find, patch, repeat.
    2. When UIs get complex — n pieces of state × m displays = n × m update paths.
    3. What UI state is — data that changes over time and affects what's shown.
    4. Synchronizing state with the DOM — duplicated truth, stale displays, ordering bugs.
    5. Declarative UI — describing outcomes instead of steps; the spreadsheet analogy.
    6. Component-based thinking — decomposition, encapsulation, reuse.
    7. React's core idea — render a description, compare, update the DOM.
    8. Components, props, state, and rendering — a first conceptual pass at all four.
    9. Why React became popular — composition, one-way data flow, ecosystem, React Native, longevity; honest trade-offs and alternatives (Vue, Svelte, Solid, Angular).
    10. Why TypeScript + React — typed contracts between every piece of UI (§3.7).

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Explain declarative vs imperative using a non-programming analogy.
    • L2 Application: Sketch the component tree for P09's UI.
    • L3 Challenge: For three bugs in your pain log, explain why they cannot happen when the UI is derived from state.
    • L4 Real-world: Write a one-page technology decision record: "React for TaskFlow Web", with alternatives considered.

    ✅ Checkpoint — Part VII · From Language to Interfaces

    • Know: how DOM types are organized; safe element selection; typed DOM events; why e.target is loosely typed; the state/DOM synchronization problem; declarative UI.
    • Build: P09 Vanilla TaskFlow, plus your pain log.
    • Answer:
      1. Why does querySelector("#id") return Element | null while querySelector("input") returns HTMLInputElement | null?
      2. What's the difference between target and currentTarget?
      3. Why does manual DOM synchronization scale badly?
      4. In one sentence, what is React's core idea?
    • Small challenge: add an "undo last delete" feature to P09. Notice how many update paths it touches.
    • Optional project: extend P09 with localStorage persistence that validates what it loads.
    • Ready signs: you can explain why React exists from your own experience, not just from the book.
    • If you struggle, revisit: Ch 35 §3–5 (selection and events), Ch 36 §2–5 (the synchronization problem).

    🛠 P09 — Vanilla TaskFlow (the pain project)

    • Difficulty: 🟡 Intermediate · When: Ch 35 · Prerequisites: Ch 35, P02
    • Concepts used: DOM types, typed events, instanceof narrowing, FormData, localStorage at a boundary, P02's domain model.
    • Requirements:
      1. A task list rendered from an in-memory array, with add, toggle, edit, and delete.
      2. Filter tabs (all/active/done), a "N left" counter, an empty state, and a "clear completed" button.
      3. Persist to localStorage; validate on load.
      4. No frameworks, and no as on DOM lookups: use narrowing helpers.
      5. Keep a PAIN-LOG.md: every synchronization bug, with how long it took to find.
    • Suggested architecture: src/state.ts (array + mutations), src/render.ts (DOM updates), src/events.ts (wiring), src/storage.ts (boundary). Try a "re-render everything" approach and a "patch only what changed" approach, and compare them.
    • Stretch goals: keyboard shortcuts; drag-to-reorder; a minimal render(state) function, discovering React's idea yourself.
    • You should understand afterward: exactly what problems React will solve for you, and what the DOM types look like underneath React's types.

    Part VIIIThinking in React

    Folder: 08-thinking-in-react/ · Roadmap: Stage 6 — Thinking in React · Difficulty: 🟢→🟡

    Purpose of the part. React as a way of thinking: rendering, snapshots, state ownership, and synchronization. Hooks are not taught as a list of APIs. State comes first (Ch 41–42), then a mental model frames every hook as the answer to a question (Ch 43), then each hook gets a chapter.

    Chapter 37The React Mental Model

    Beginner Essential 37-react-mental-model/

    Opens with: P09's "toggle a task" handler (35 lines of DOM patching) next to the React version (8 lines, zero DOM calls). Mental model: 🧠 UI = f(state). A render is React calling your component function to get a description; a commit is React applying the differences to the DOM. You describe; React updates.

    1. Setting up React with Vite and TypeScript — the react-ts template, file tour, dev server.
    2. UI as a function of state — the core equation, demonstrated.
    3. Components return descriptions — elements are plain objects, not DOM nodes.
    4. Trigger, render, commit — the three steps of every update.
    5. The render tree — parents re-render children; what "re-render" does not mean (DOM replacement).
    6. Purity — components must be pure during render; why Strict Mode renders twice in development.
    7. What React is and isn't — a UI library, not a framework; where routing and data fit later.
    8. React DevTools — inspecting components, props, and state.

    Common mistakes: thinking a re-render rewrites the DOM · side effects during render · mutating props.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Label trigger/render/commit in three scenarios.
    • L2 Application: Port P09's static task list markup into a component tree.
    • L3 Challenge: Write an impure component, observe the Strict Mode double render, and fix it.
    • L4 Real-world: Explore a production React site with DevTools and sketch its component hierarchy.

    Chapter 38JSX: Describing UI with JavaScript

    Beginner Essential 38-jsx/

    Opens with: "Is JSX HTML?" The compiled output of <Button kind="primary">Save</Button>, shown as a function call. Mental model: JSX is syntax for creating element objects. Anything you can do with JavaScript expressions, you can do in braces.

    1. JSX is JavaScript — compilation to jsx() calls; why one root element.
    2. Expressions in braces — values, function calls, conditionals.
    3. Attributes become props — className, htmlFor, style objects, camelCase handlers.
    4. Fragments — grouping without wrapper elements.
    5. What renders and what doesn't — null, undefined, and false render nothing; 0 renders "0".
    6. JSX and safety — automatic escaping; why dangerouslySetInnerHTML is named that way.
    7. TSX specifics — .tsx files, no angle-bracket assertions, <T,> for generic arrow functions.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Translate five JSX snippets to jsx() calls and back.
    • L2 Application: Convert an HTML template to JSX, fixing every attribute.
    • L3 Challenge: Explain why {items.length && <List />} can render a stray 0.
    • L4 Real-world: Build a static product page from a design mockup.

    Chapter 39Components, Props & Composition

    Beginner Essential 39-components-props-composition/

    Opens with: one 300-line App component that does everything. Mental model: Components are functions; props are their arguments; children are a special argument that holds nested UI. Data flows down and events flow up.

    1. Defining components — naming, one concept per component, files.
    2. Props as parameters — destructuring, a simple props type, defaults.
    3. Children — nesting UI, wrapper components.
    4. Composition over configuration — small composable parts vs "mega-prop" components.
    5. Passing callbacks — child-to-parent communication.
    6. One-way data flow — data down, events up.
    7. Splitting a UI into components — from mockup to hierarchy (Thinking in React, step 1).
    8. Styling components (orientation) — CSS Modules, utility CSS, inline styles; the decision is deferred to Ch 58 and Ch 93.

    Common mistakes: components that are too big or too small · copying props into state · boolean-prop explosion (isPrimary isLarge isRounded…). Project: P10 Component Gallery (begins here).

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Extract three components from a provided page.
    • L2 Application: Build a Card that composes Card.Header-style children through props and children.
    • L3 Challenge: Refactor a 12-prop component into composable pieces.
    • L4 Real-world: Decompose a real app screen (e.g., an email client) into a component tree with data flow arrows.

    Chapter 40Conditional Rendering, Lists & Keys

    Beginner Essential 40-conditionals-lists-keys/

    Opens with: deleting the second item in a list, after which the third item's half-typed input text jumps into the second row. Mental model: 🧠 A key is an item's identity across renders. React matches elements by position and key, not by content.

    1. Conditional rendering patterns — early return, ternary, &&, lookup objects.
    2. The && pitfall — numbers and empty strings.
    3. Rendering lists — map, filtering and sorting before rendering.
    4. Keys and identity — what React does with keys during reconciliation.
    5. Key mistakes — index keys, random keys, unstable keys.
    6. Keys as a reset tool — key={userId} to reset a subtree's state.
    7. Empty states — designing for "nothing to show" from the start.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Choose correct keys for five data sets.
    • L2 Application: Render TaskFlow tasks grouped by status with headings and empty states.
    • L3 Challenge: Reproduce the "jumping input" bug with index keys, then fix it.
    • L4 Real-world: Build a searchable, sortable contact list with highlighted matches.

    Chapter 41Interactivity: Events & State

    Beginner Essential 41-events-and-state/

    Opens with: let count = 0; <button onClick={() => count++}> that never updates the screen. Mental model: 🧠 State is a component's memory, and every render sees a snapshot of it. Setting state doesn't change the current snapshot; it schedules a new render with a new one.

    1. Responding to events — handlers, passing vs calling, the event object.
    2. Why local variables don't work — they reset each render and don't trigger renders.
    3. useState — declaring state; the [value, setValue] tuple.
    4. State as a snapshot — why console.log(count) after setCount shows the old value.
    5. Batching and updater functions — setCount(c => c + 1) and when you need it.
    6. Updating objects in state — immutability, spreading, nested updates.
    7. Updating arrays in state — map, filter, and spread instead of push/splice.
    8. Event propagation — bubbling, stopPropagation, preventDefault.

    Common mistakes: mutating state · expecting synchronous updates · calling the handler instead of passing it (onClick={save()}).

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Predict the displayed value after three setCount patterns.
    • L2 Application: Build add/toggle/delete for tasks with immutable updates.
    • L3 Challenge: Implement "move task up/down" without mutation.
    • L4 Real-world: Build a shopping cart with quantities, removal, and a computed total.

    Chapter 42Thinking in State: Structure, Derivation & Lifting

    Intermediate Essential 42-thinking-in-state/

    Opens with: a component storing tasks, doneTasks, doneCount, and hasTasks. Four pieces of state that disagree after one bug. Mental model: 🧠 Store the minimum; derive the rest. Every piece of data has exactly one owner, the closest common parent of everything that needs it.

    1. Minimal state — what not to store.
    2. Derived values — computing during render instead of syncing.
    3. Principles of state structure — group related state, avoid contradictions, redundancy, duplication, and deep nesting.
    4. Controlled and uncontrolled inputs — value + onChange vs defaultValue.
    5. Lifting state up — moving state to the common parent.
    6. Sharing state between siblings — via the parent.
    7. State colocation — keep state as low as possible, as high as necessary.
    8. Preserving and resetting state — how tree position and keys decide it.
    9. Thinking in React, end to end — the five steps applied to a filterable task board.

    Common mistakes: syncing derived state with effects · duplicating server data into local state · lifting everything to App.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Identify redundant state in four components.
    • L2 Application: Lift the filter state so both the tabs and the counter use it.
    • L3 Challenge: Refactor a "state soup" component to minimal state with derived values.
    • L4 Real-world: Build a two-pane email-style UI (list + detail) with correct state ownership.

    Chapter 43Hooks: The Mental Model

    Intermediate Essential 43-hooks-mental-model/

    Opens with: a hook called inside an if, and the bizarre bug where one state variable shows another's value. Mental model: 🧠 React gives each component instance a list of memory slots, and hooks claim them in call order on every render. That is why the rules exist.

    Question you're asking Hook that answers it Chapter
    "I need to remember something that affects what's shown." useState 41
    "I need to remember something that doesn't affect what's shown." useRef 45
    "I need to synchronize with something outside React." useEffect 44
    "I need data from far up the tree." useContext 46
    "My state changes follow complex rules." useReducer 55
    "I need to skip expensive work or keep identity stable." useMemo / useCallback 47
    "I want to reuse a combination of the above." A custom hook 48
    1. What a hook is — a function that hooks into React's per-component memory.
    2. The rules of hooks, and why — call-order slots; top level only; React functions only.
    3. The question → hook map — the table above, with one tiny example each.
    4. Hooks compose — custom hooks are made of hooks.
    5. Hooks and the render cycle — what runs during render vs after commit.
    6. Linting the rules — eslint-plugin-react-hooks errors as teachers.
    7. The React Compiler, briefly — what it automates and what you still need to understand.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Match ten scenarios to the right hook.
    • L2 Application: Find and fix three rules-of-hooks violations.
    • L3 Challenge: Explain, with a diagram of memory slots, why a conditional hook breaks.
    • L4 Real-world: Annotate an existing component: for each hook, the "question" it answers.

    Chapter 44useEffect: Synchronizing with the Outside World

    Intermediate Essential 44-effects/

    Opens with: a chat room component that connects twice, never disconnects, and shows messages from the previous room after switching. Mental model: 🧠 An effect is a synchronization: "while this component is on screen with these values, keep this external thing in sync". Setup starts it, cleanup stops it, and dependencies decide when to restart.

    1. Effects are for synchronization — not "lifecycle methods".
    2. Anatomy of an effect — setup, cleanup, dependencies.
    3. The dependency array — reactive values; the lint rule as the source of truth.
    4. Cleanup — subscriptions, timers, and aborting requests.
    5. Strict Mode's double effect — why mount → unmount → mount exposes missing cleanups.
    6. Fetching in an effect — race conditions, AbortController, stale responses.
    7. You might not need an effect — derived values, event handlers, resetting with keys.
    8. Separating events from effects — non-reactive logic with useEffectEvent.
    9. Common effect bugs — infinite loops, stale closures, object dependencies.

    Common mistakes: suppressing the dependency lint · effects that set derived state · fetching without cleanup. When not to: anything triggered by a user action belongs in an event handler.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Classify eight pieces of logic as "render", "event handler", or "effect".
    • L2 Application: Sync document.title with the number of open tasks.
    • L3 Challenge: Fix a racing search-as-you-type fetch with AbortController.
    • L4 Real-world: Build a reconnecting WebSocket status indicator with correct cleanup.

    Chapter 45useRef: Remembering Without Re-rendering

    Intermediate Essential 45-refs/

    Opens with: a stopwatch whose setInterval ID is stored in state, causing extra renders, or in a variable, so it's lost on the next render. Mental model: A ref is a mutable box that survives renders but doesn't trigger them. React gives you the same box every render.

    1. Refs vs state — when changes should and shouldn't re-render.
    2. Storing values across renders — timer IDs, previous values, instance counters.
    3. Referencing DOM elements — focus, scroll, measure.
    4. Managing focus — accessible focus after actions (deepened in Ch 73).
    5. Ref pitfalls — reading or writing refs during render.
    6. Refs as props — passing refs to your own components (typed in Ch 53).

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Choose state or ref for six values.
    • L2 Application: Focus the "new task" input after adding a task.
    • L3 Challenge: Build usePrevious(value) and explain its timing.
    • L4 Real-world: Build a stopwatch with lap times and no unnecessary renders.

    Chapter 46useContext: Sharing Data Through the Tree

    Intermediate Essential 46-context/

    Opens with: theme and currentUser threaded through six layers of components that don't use them. Mental model: Context is a broadcast channel scoped to a subtree: a provider sends, and any descendant can tune in.

    1. The prop-drilling problem — when it's fine and when it hurts.
    2. Creating and providing context — createContext, providers.
    3. Consuming context — useContext, the nearest provider wins.
    4. Context with state — provider components that own state.
    5. When to use context — theme, auth, locale, feature-level state; not "everything global".
    6. Context and re-renders — splitting contexts, stable values.
    7. Composition before context — passing components as children to avoid drilling.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Decide context vs props for six data items.
    • L2 Application: Add a theme context with a toggle.
    • L3 Challenge: Remove a prop-drilling chain using composition alone, with no context.
    • L4 Real-world: Design the context map for TaskFlow (what lives where, and why).

    Chapter 47useMemo, useCallback & memo: Identity and Performance

    Intermediate Essential 47-memoization/

    Opens with: a memoized child that re-renders anyway, because its onSelect prop is a new function every render. Mental model: 🧠 Every render creates new objects and functions. Memoization keeps the previous one when inputs haven't changed, trading memory and complexity for skipped work.

    1. Referential identity — {} !== {}; functions are new every render.
    2. When re-renders are a problem — and when they aren't; measure first.
    3. memo — skipping a child's render when its props are equal.
    4. useMemo — caching expensive computations and stable objects.
    5. useCallback — stable function identities.
    6. The cost of memoization — complexity, dependency bugs, wasted comparisons.
    7. The React Compiler — automatic memoization and how it changes the defaults.
    8. A decision checklist — profile, then memoize the proven bottleneck.

    When not to: by default, don't. Add memoization when a profiler shows a problem, or when identity matters (effect dependencies, memoized children).

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Predict which children re-render in four scenarios.
    • L2 Application: Make a memoized list item actually skip renders.
    • L3 Challenge: Remove unnecessary useMemo/useCallback from a component without changing behavior or performance.
    • L4 Real-world: Profile a slow filterable list of 5,000 items and fix the real bottleneck.

    Chapter 48Custom Hooks: Reusing Stateful Logic

    Intermediate Essential 48-custom-hooks/

    Opens with: the same "sync with localStorage" logic copy-pasted into four components, each with a slightly different bug. Mental model: A custom hook is a function that uses hooks, so it gets its own state slots in each component that calls it. Hooks share logic, not state.

    1. Extracting a custom hook — from duplication to useSomething.
    2. Naming and rules — the use prefix and why the linter cares.
    3. Logic, not state — two components using the same hook get independent state.
    4. Designing a hook's interface — inputs, outputs, tuple vs object returns (typed deeply in Ch 56).
    5. Common custom hooks — useLocalStorage, useDebouncedValue, useMediaQuery, useOnlineStatus.
    6. When not to make a hook — premature extraction; hooks that hide simple code.
    7. Testing hooks (preview) — why hooks are testable units (Ch 67).

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Identify logic in three components that could become a hook.
    • L2 Application: Write useToggle and useDebouncedValue.
    • L3 Challenge: Write useLocalStorage that handles invalid stored JSON safely (runtime safety, again).
    • L4 Real-world: Extract TaskFlow's filtering and keyboard-shortcut logic into hooks.

    ✅ Checkpoint — Part VIII · Thinking in React

    • Know: render vs commit; purity; JSX; components, props, children, composition; conditional rendering; keys; state snapshots; immutable updates; minimal and derived state; lifting state; the hooks mental model; effects as synchronization; refs; context; memoization trade-offs; custom hooks.
    • Build: P10 Component Gallery and P11 TaskFlow in React.
    • Answer:
      1. Why does console.log(state) right after setState print the old value?
      2. What problem do keys solve, and why are index keys risky?
      3. Give two examples of logic that should not be in an effect.
      4. Why do the rules of hooks exist?
      5. When is useMemo worth it?
      6. What's the difference between sharing logic (custom hooks) and sharing state (lifting, context)?
    • Small challenge: build a debounced search box over a list, with correct effect cleanup and no unnecessary state.
    • Optional project: add undo/redo to P11.
    • Ready signs: you design state ownership before writing components; you rarely write effects for derived data.
    • If you struggle, revisit: Ch 41 §4 (snapshots), Ch 42 (state structure), Ch 44 §1–7 (effects), Ch 43 (the hooks model).

    🛠 P10 — Component Gallery (basic React components)

    • Difficulty: 🟢 Beginner · When: Ch 39–42 · Prerequisites: Ch 37–42
    • Concepts used: components, props, children, composition, conditional rendering, lists and keys, state, events, controlled inputs.
    • Requirements:
      1. Eight components: Button, Badge, Avatar (image with initials fallback), Card, Toggle, Counter, Tabs, Accordion.
      2. A gallery page with a sidebar listing every component and 2–3 variants each.
      3. Props typed with simple type aliases; no any.
      4. Tabs and Accordion manage their own state; the gallery's selected component lives in the URL hash.
    • Suggested architecture: src/components/<Name>/<Name>.tsx + index.ts; src/gallery/GalleryPage.tsx.
    • Stretch goals: keyboard support for Tabs (arrow keys); a theme toggle (to be replaced by context after Ch 46).
    • You should understand afterward: decomposition, composition, and component-level state ownership. These components get redesigned with proper API types in Ch 50 and again as a library in P20.

    🛠 P11 — TaskFlow in React

    • Difficulty: 🟡 Intermediate · When: end of Part VIII · Prerequisites: Part VIII, P02, P09
    • Concepts used: everything in Part VIII.
    • Requirements:
      1. Re-implement all of P09's features in React.
      2. Persist with a validated useLocalStorage hook.
      3. Keyboard shortcuts via an effect with cleanup; focus management via refs.
      4. A theme context.
      5. Write a RETRO.md comparing P09 and P11: lines of code, number of sync bugs, time to add the "clear completed" feature.
    • Suggested architecture:
      src/
  features/tasks/{components,hooks}/
  domain/          # reused from P02
  shared/{components,hooks,context}/
    • Stretch goals: drag-and-drop reordering; undo; a Profiler experiment before and after memoization.
    • You should understand afterward: the measured payoff of declarative UI, in your own numbers.

    Part IXReact + TypeScript

    Folder: 09-react-typescript/ · Roadmap: Stage 7 — React with TypeScript · Difficulty: 🟡 · ⭐ Major milestone

    Purpose of the part. Part VIII taught what props, state, and hooks are. Part IX teaches how to type them well: contracts that catch misuse, model UI states precisely, and keep inference doing the work. Every chapter revisits a Book One concept in its React form.

    Chapter 49How TypeScript Sees React: JSX, Elements & Component Types

    Intermediate Essential 49-how-typescript-sees-react/

    Opens with: three components returning JSX.Element, ReactElement, and ReactNode, and a children prop that rejects a string. What do these types actually mean? Mental model: 🧠 JSX type-checking is ordinary type-checking: <Button kind="x" /> is a function call, and TypeScript checks the attributes against the component's props type like any other argument.

    1. How JSX is type-checked — the jsx setting, the React.JSX namespace, intrinsic elements.
    2. Where React's types come from — @types/react, keeping it aligned with your React version.
    3. ReactNode vs ReactElement vs JSX.Element — what a component can return and what children can hold.
    4. Typing function components — plain functions with typed props; React.FC and why this book doesn't use it.
    5. Intrinsic element props — ComponentProps<"button">, ComponentPropsWithoutRef, ComponentPropsWithRef.
    6. Reading React's type definitions — go-to-definition into @types/react; reading what you find.
    7. 🕰 Legacy types you'll meet — implicit children in React.FC (pre-18), defaultProps, PropTypes, forwardRef, the global JSX namespace.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Classify ten values as valid ReactNode, ReactElement, both, or neither.
    • L2 Application: Retype the P10 components without React.FC.
    • L3 Challenge: Find the props type of <input> in @types/react and list five props you didn't know existed.
    • L4 Real-world: Upgrade a small React 17-era component file to modern types; document each change.

    Chapter 50Typing Props & Component APIs

    Intermediate Essential 50-typing-props/

    Opens with: a Button that accepts onClick, but not type="submit", disabled, or aria-label, until someone adds [key: string]: any and loses everything. Mental model: 🧠 A component's props type is its public API. Design it like a function signature: small, consistent, hard to misuse, and extending native elements wherever the component is one.

    1. Props types — alias vs interface for props; naming conventions.
    2. Optional props and defaults — default values in destructuring (defaultProps is gone for function components).
    3. Typing children — ReactNode, required vs optional children, PropsWithChildren, and why you can't constrain children types usefully.
    4. Callback props — onSelect: (id: TaskId) => void; onX vs handleX naming.
    5. Slot props — icon?: ReactNode, header: ReactNode, and render-function props (preview).
    6. Extending native elements — ComponentProps<"button"> & {…}, Omit for overrides, spreading ...rest.
    7. Discriminated props (first look) — variant: "link" requires href (deep dive in Ch 85).
    8. Designing component APIs — consistency, controlled vs uncontrolled, sensible defaults; redesigning P10's APIs.

    Common mistakes: index signatures on props · re-declaring native props by hand · boolean flags that should be a union (size: "sm" | "md" | "lg"). When not to: don't extend every native prop for components that aren't wrappers of a native element.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Type props for five components from their descriptions.
    • L2 Application: Build a Button that accepts all native button props plus variant and size.
    • L3 Challenge: Build a TextField with label, error, hint, and all native input props, with correct id wiring.
    • L4 Real-world: Write an API review of three P10 components and ship the improved versions.

    Chapter 51Typing Events

    Intermediate Essential 51-typing-events/

    Opens with: function handleChange(e: any) copied across a codebase, and a bug where e.target.value was read from the wrong element. Mental model: React events are typed wrappers around DOM events: React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement> = "a change event whose currentTarget is an input". Inline handlers get their types for free through contextual typing.

    1. Synthetic events — React's event system and where its types live.
    2. Inline handlers and contextual typing — why inline needs no annotation.
    3. Extracted handlers — (e: React.MouseEvent<HTMLButtonElement>) => void vs MouseEventHandler<HTMLButtonElement>.
    4. Mouse and pointer events
    5. Keyboard events — e.key, typed key unions for shortcuts.
    6. Change events — inputs, selects, textareas, checkboxes (checked).
    7. Form and submit events — FormEvent<HTMLFormElement>, preventDefault, FormData from currentTarget.
    8. Focus events — onFocus, onBlur, relatedTarget.
    9. target vs currentTarget in React — the Ch 35 lesson, in its React form.
    10. Discovering event types — hover the prop; ComponentProps<"input">["onChange"].

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Write the handler type for eight elements/events.
    • L2 Application: Implement keyboard shortcuts (n, /, Escape) with a typed key map.
    • L3 Challenge: Write one handler that serves several inputs using name and a typed state object.
    • L4 Real-world: Remove every any-typed handler from a provided legacy component set.

    Chapter 52Typing State: Modeling UI States

    Intermediate Essential 52-typing-state/

    Opens with: const [user, setUser] = useState(null), and every later setUser(data) fails with Argument of type 'User' is not assignable to parameter of type 'null'. Mental model: useState is a generic function: TypeScript infers T from the initial value, so when the initial value doesn't represent every future value, tell it T.

    1. useState inference — primitives, objects, arrays.
    2. Explicit state types — useState<Task[]>([]); when inference is too narrow.
    3. Nullable state — useState<User | null>(null) and narrowing before use.
    4. Union state — useState<"idle" | "saving" | "saved">("idle").
    5. Object and array state — typed immutable updates, Partial<T> update helpers.
    6. Discriminated state — async status as a union, rendered exhaustively.
    7. Lazy initial state — useState(() => loadDraft()) with typed loaders.
    8. From boolean soup to a state machine — refactoring isLoading/isError/data.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Give the inferred T for eight useState calls.
    • L2 Application: Type a file-upload component's state as a discriminated union.
    • L3 Challenge: Refactor a component with five boolean flags into one union state.
    • L4 Real-world: Model a multi-step checkout's state so you can't reach "payment" without a shipping address.

    Chapter 53Typing Refs

    Intermediate Essential 53-typing-refs/

    Opens with: inputRef.current.focus() → 'inputRef.current' is possibly 'null'. Why can't a ref just be the element? Mental model: A DOM ref is empty during the first render and filled in after commit, so its type honestly includes null. A value ref holds whatever you put in it.

    1. DOM refs — useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null) and narrowing before use.
    2. Mutable value refs — useRef<number | null>(null) for timer IDs, useRef(0) for counters.
    3. Modern ref typings — useRef requires an argument; RefObject is mutable.
    4. Refs as props — passing ref to your own function components; Ref<HTMLInputElement> and ComponentProps<"input">.
    5. Callback refs — (node: HTMLDivElement | null) => void, and cleanup functions.
    6. 🕰 forwardRef in existing code — reading and typing forwardRef<HTMLInputElement, Props>, then migrating away.
    7. useImperativeHandle — exposing a small typed handle ({ focus(): void; reset(): void }).
    8. Merging refs — combining an internal ref with one passed in.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Write the correct useRef call for six uses.
    • L2 Application: Build a TextField that accepts a ref and forwards it to the input.
    • L3 Challenge: Expose a typed scrollToItem(id) handle from a list component.
    • L4 Real-world: Migrate three forwardRef components to ref-as-prop, keeping their public types identical.

    Chapter 54Typed Context

    Intermediate Essential 54-typed-context/

    Opens with: createContext<AuthValue>({} as AuthValue), a lie that compiles and then crashes when someone forgets the provider. Mental model: 🧠 A context's type should tell the truth about the case where no provider exists. Make "no provider" impossible to ignore by funneling all access through a custom hook that throws.

    1. createContext typing — the type parameter and the default value.
    2. The default value problem — fake defaults vs honest null/undefined.
    3. The safe context pattern — createContext<Value | null>(null) plus useAuth() that throws outside its provider.
    4. Typed provider components — provider props, memoized values.
    5. Consumers through hooks — the custom hook as the only consumer API.
    6. Context + reducer — typed state and dispatch contexts.
    7. Splitting contexts — separating state from actions for fewer re-renders.
    8. Modern context syntax — <Context value={…}> as the provider, and reading context with use.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Identify the unsafe pattern in four context definitions.
    • L2 Application: Build a typed ThemeContext with the safe pattern.
    • L3 Challenge: Write a createSafeContext<T>(name) helper returning [Provider, useValue].
    • L4 Real-world: Build TaskFlow's NotificationsContext (toasts) with a typed API: notify({ kind, message }).

    Chapter 55Reducers & State Machines with Discriminated Unions

    Intermediate Essential 55-reducers/

    Opens with: a task board with seven useState calls and update logic spread across eleven handlers. One handler forgets to reset selectedId. Mental model: 🧠 A reducer is a pure function (state, action) => newState. Actions are a discriminated union, the "events" that can happen. Exhaustive switch means adding an event forces you to handle it.

    1. When transitions get complex — the signals that you need a reducer.
    2. useReducer — state, action, dispatch; reducers as pure functions.
    3. Actions as discriminated unions — { type: "taskAdded"; task } | { type: "taskRemoved"; id }.
    4. Exhaustive reducers — switch + assertNever; compile errors for unhandled actions.
    5. Modeling state and actions together — state machines with status-dependent data.
    6. Typed dispatch helpers — action creators, Dispatch<Action>.
    7. Reducer + context — app-level state without a library.
    8. Testing reducers — pure functions are the easiest code to test.

    Common mistakes: actions with optional payload fields instead of separate members · reducers with side effects · one mega-reducer for the whole app.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Write the action union for a counter with step, reset, and set.
    • L2 Application: Convert P11's task state to a reducer with exhaustive handling.
    • L3 Challenge: Model a media player (idle, loading, playing, paused, error) where invalid transitions are ignored by design.
    • L4 Real-world: Add undo/redo to the reducer generically (withUndo(reducer)).

    Chapter 56Typing Custom Hooks

    Intermediate Essential 56-typing-custom-hooks/

    Opens with: const [value, setValue] = useToggle() where value is inferred as boolean | (() => void). Why did the tuple fall apart? Mental model: A custom hook is a function, so type it like a public function: precise parameters, deliberate return types, and generics only where a caller's type must flow through.

    1. Typed parameters — options objects and their defaults.
    2. Typed return values — tuples with as const vs objects; when to use each.
    3. Inferred vs explicit return types — hooks as public APIs.
    4. Generic custom hooks — useLocalStorage<T>(key, initial), with T inferred from initial.
    5. Parsers instead of lies — useFetch<T>(url) is a lying generic; require parse: (data: unknown) => T.
    6. Reusable hook APIs — stable callbacks, options objects, documentation.
    7. Typing hooks that wrap libraries — deriving types from library functions (Parameters, ReturnType).
    8. Type tests for hooks — locking down a hook's public types.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Fix the tuple inference in three hooks.
    • L2 Application: Write useLocalStorage<T> with a parser and schema support.
    • L3 Challenge: Write useAsync<T>(fn) returning a discriminated state union.
    • L4 Real-world: Build useKeyboardShortcuts(map) with a typed shortcut map and cleanup, with tests.

    Chapter 57Generic Components: The Essentials

    Advanced Essential 57-generic-components/

    Opens with: a Select whose onChange gives back string, so every caller re-finds the object it already had. Mental model: A generic component is a generic function that returns UI: the items you pass decide T, and every callback receives T back.

    1. Why generic components — keeping the caller's type through the component.
    2. Declaring a generic component — function List<T>(props: ListProps<T>); <T,> in arrow functions.
    3. Inference from props — items decides T; render callbacks receive T.
    4. Constraining T — T extends { id: string } for keys.
    5. A generic Select — getLabel, getKey, onChange(value: T).
    6. Limits and pitfalls — generics with memo, with context, and explicit <List<Task> … /> arguments.
    7. When not to — single-use components; when a simple union of props suffices.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Make a List generic so renderItem receives the right type.
    • L2 Application: Build Select<T> used for both projects and users.
    • L3 Challenge: Make a generic Table<T> with typed columns (the start of P19).
    • L4 Real-world: Replace three near-duplicate list components in P12 with one generic component.

    ✅ Checkpoint — Part IX · React + TypeScript ⭐

    • Know: JSX type-checking; ReactNode vs ReactElement; props design; native prop extension; event types; state inference vs explicit types; union and discriminated state; ref typing (DOM, value, ref-as-prop, callback refs); safe context; reducers with exhaustive actions; custom hook typing; generic components.
    • Build: P12 React Dashboard.
    • Answer:
      1. Why is ReactNode the right type for children in most components?
      2. How do you type a component that should accept every native <button> prop plus your own?
      3. Why does useState(null) cause problems, and what are two fixes?
      4. Why does a DOM ref's type include null?
      5. What's wrong with createContext({} as Value)?
      6. What does exhaustiveness checking buy you in a reducer?
    • Small challenge: build a fully typed Modal (open state, onClose, focus on open, Escape to close, a ref to the dialog) in 45 minutes.
    • Optional project: retype and redesign all of P10 as a mini design system.
    • Ready signs: you no longer write any in components; your props types read like documentation.
    • If you struggle, revisit: Ch 13–14 (unions and narrowing, which most React typing problems come down to), Ch 16–18 (generics), Ch 50, 52, 54.

    🛠 P12 — React Dashboard

    • Difficulty: 🟡 Intermediate · When: end of Part IX · Prerequisites: Part IX
    • Concepts used: typed props, events, union state, refs, safe context, reducer + context, typed custom hooks, generic components.
    • Requirements:
      1. A dashboard shell: sidebar, header, theme toggle, responsive grid.
      2. Four widgets: KPI cards, a task-status chart (any chart library), a recent-activity list, and a team-workload table.
      3. Global filters (date range, project, assignee) managed by a typed reducer + context.
      4. Each widget renders loading | error | empty | ready from a discriminated union (data from validated static JSON with simulated latency).
      5. Generic Select<T> and List<T> used by at least two widgets each.
      6. No any, no as outside a single documented boundary module.
    • Suggested architecture:
      src/
  app/            # shell, providers, theme
  features/dashboard/{widgets,filters,hooks,types}/
  shared/{ui,hooks,lib}/
  data/           # static JSON + schemas (boundary)
    • Stretch goals: filters synced to the URL; a draggable widget layout; keyboard-accessible chart summaries.
    • You should understand afterward: typed component APIs at small-app scale; context + reducer architecture. P17 evolves this into a production dashboard.

    Part XBuilding Real Applications

    Folder: 10-building-real-applications/ · Roadmap: Stage 8 — Real Applications · Difficulty: 🟡→🟠

    Purpose of the part. From components to applications. The reader structures a multi-page app, decides where every piece of state lives, crosses the network boundary safely, builds forms with shared schemas, and adds authentication. Throughout, TypeScript is the tool that makes layer boundaries explicit: DTOs at the network edge, domain types in the middle, and view props at the UI.

     UI components ──props──► feature hooks ──domain types──► services ──DTOs──► API client ──► network
      ▲                         ▲                              ▲                    ▲
  view models             query/mutation hooks          mappers (DTO → domain)  schemas (unknown → DTO)

    Chapter 58Architecting a React Application

    Intermediate Essential 58-application-architecture/

    Opens with: TaskFlow at 60 components in a flat components/ folder. Every change touches five unrelated files, and two developers keep editing the same ones. Mental model: 🧠 Organize by feature, depend in one direction, and expose each feature through a small public API. Types are the contracts at each seam.

    1. Why structure matters — change cost, ownership, onboarding.
    2. By type vs by feature — trade-offs and a recommended hybrid.
    3. Feature modules — components/, hooks/, api/, types.ts, and an index.ts public API.
    4. Layers in a frontend — UI → hooks → services → API client → network.
    5. Where types live — domain types, DTOs, view models; what goes in shared/types.
    6. Dependency rules — features don't import each other's internals; enforced with lint rules.
    7. Shared components — shared/ui primitives vs feature components.
    8. Environment configuration — typing import.meta.env (declaration merging, Ch 28), a validated env module, and which variables are exposed to the browser.
    9. A styling strategy — choosing CSS Modules or utility CSS for the app, and why consistency matters more than the choice.
    10. Scaffolding TaskFlow Web — the structure for P14.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Sort twelve files into a feature-based structure.
    • L2 Application: Add a lint rule that forbids importing another feature's internals.
    • L3 Challenge: Refactor P11 from a flat layout into features without breaking tests.
    • L4 Real-world: Write an architecture decision record for TaskFlow Web's structure.

    Chapter 59Routing & Navigation

    Intermediate Essential 59-routing/

    Opens with: a "single-page" app where refresh loses your place, the back button exits the site, and nothing can be bookmarked. Mental model: The URL is state, and the most shareable state you have. Routes map URL patterns to UI; params and search params are untrusted input.

    1. Why routing — URLs as state; SPA navigation.
    2. Routes, nested routes, and layouts — with React Router.
    3. Route params and their types — string | undefined; parsing and validating params.
    4. Search params as state — filters and pagination in the URL, validated with schemas.
    5. Navigation — links, programmatic navigation, redirects.
    6. Not-found and error routes
    7. Lazy routes — splitting by route (preview of Ch 70).
    8. Type-safe routing — typed route helpers from an as const route map; type-safe routers (TanStack Router) and route type generation as alternatives.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Define routes for a 6-page app with nested layouts.
    • L2 Application: Parse /projects/:projectId/tasks/:taskId params with a schema and render a not-found state for invalid IDs.
    • L3 Challenge: Keep table filters in search params with validation and defaults.
    • L4 Real-world: Build TaskFlow Web's routing with a typed href() helper that rejects unknown routes.

    Chapter 60Where State Lives: State Management Architecture

    Intermediate Essential 60-state-management/

    Opens with: a global store containing the current user, every task from the server, the open modal, and the text in a search box. One update triggers hundreds of re-renders and a stale-data bug. Mental model: 🧠 There are five kinds of state, and each has a natural home: local UI (component), shared client (context/store), URL (router), server cache (a server-state library), form (form state).

    1. The five kinds of state — examples of each from TaskFlow.
    2. Server state is not client state — it's a cache of someone else's data: staleness, refetching, ownership.
    3. Choosing a home — a decision flowchart.
    4. Context + reducer at app scale — where it works and where it strains.
    5. External stores — a typed Zustand store with selectors; an overview of Redux Toolkit.
    6. Derived state across features — selectors and computed values.
    7. Avoiding global-state sprawl — colocate first, promote only when needed.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Classify fifteen pieces of TaskFlow state into the five kinds.
    • L2 Application: Move the "open modal" state out of a global store into local state.
    • L3 Challenge: Implement a typed Zustand store with slices and selectors, with tests.
    • L4 Real-world: Write TaskFlow Web's state map: every piece of state, its home, and its reason.

    Chapter 61Data Fetching & the API Boundary

    Advanced Essential 61-data-fetching/

    Opens with: a component typed useState<Task[]>, a fetch with as Task[], and a production crash because the server started returning { items: Task[], nextCursor }. Mental model: 🧠 "What TypeScript believes" is your types. "What the server actually returned" is unknown. The only bridge between them is a parser at the boundary.

                 what TypeScript believes          what the server actually returned
  const tasks: Task[] = await res.json();     { "items": [...], "nextCursor": "abc" }
                         ▲                                   │
                         └──── any → Task[]  (no check!) ────┘     ✗ crash later, far away

  const tasks = TaskListSchema.parse(await res.json());          ✓ fails here, loudly, with details
    1. What TypeScript believes vs what the server returned — the crash, reproduced.
    2. DTOs vs domain models on the client — why the UI shouldn't depend on the wire format.
    3. Reusing the typed API client — P08 inside a React app.
    4. Validating responses — schemas at the boundary; what to do when validation fails.
    5. Transforming API responses — mappers (string dates → Date, cents → money, nested → flat).
    6. Typing API errors — the ApiError union mapped to user-facing messages.
    7. Loading, error, empty, and success states — one union, rendered exhaustively; skeletons.
    8. A hand-rolled useQuery — and the pain it reveals: caching, deduplication, races, refetching.
    9. Request types and mutations — typed bodies, pending states, and a first look at optimistic UI.

    Common mistakes: as on responses · DTO types leaking into components · treating "empty" as "error".

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Mark every boundary in a provided data-flow diagram.
    • L2 Application: Add response validation and a mapper to one TaskFlow endpoint.
    • L3 Challenge: Build useQuery-lite with abort-on-change and a tiny cache; list what's still missing.
    • L4 Real-world: Handle a breaking API change (field renamed) so it shows a clear error state instead of a white screen.

    Chapter 62Server State with TanStack Query

    Advanced Essential 62-server-state/

    Opens with: the hand-rolled hook from Ch 61, now with three cache bugs and a stale list after creating a task. Mental model: A server-state library is a cache with rules: queries read and share data by key; mutations change the server and invalidate keys.

    1. What a server-state library solves — the Ch 61 pain list, item by item.
    2. Queries — useQuery types inferred from the query function.
    3. Query keys — typed key factories and queryOptions for reuse.
    4. Mutations — useMutation and invalidation.
    5. Optimistic updates — typed rollback context.
    6. Suspense queries and error boundaries — useSuspenseQuery.
    7. Pagination and infinite queries
    8. Devtools and testing — inspecting the cache; testing with a fresh client.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Design query keys for tasks, task detail, and filtered lists.
    • L2 Application: Replace the hand-rolled hook with queries and mutations.
    • L3 Challenge: Implement optimistic task completion with rollback on failure.
    • L4 Real-world: Add cursor-based infinite scrolling to the task list.

    Chapter 63Typed Forms from Scratch

    Intermediate Essential 63-typed-forms/

    Opens with: a sign-up form with six useState calls, a handleChange(e: any), and validation logic duplicated in three places. Mental model: A form is a small state machine over a typed values object: values, touched, errors, and submission status. Field names are keyof Values, so a typo is a compile error.

    1. Typed form state — a FormValues type and initial values.
    2. Form events — change, blur, and submit, typed (from Ch 51).
    3. A typed change handler — name as keyof FormValues.
    4. Submission — async submit, disabling, and preventing double submission.
    5. Client-side validation — validators returning FormErrors<T> (the mapped type from Ch 22).
    6. Touched, dirty, and error display — when to show which message.
    7. Accessible forms — labels, aria-invalid, aria-describedby, focusing the first error.
    8. Building useForm — a type-safe form hook by hand.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Type the values and errors for a login form.
    • L2 Application: Build a create-task form with validation and accessible errors.
    • L3 Challenge: Implement useForm<T> with register(name) returning typed input props.
    • L4 Real-world: Build a multi-step project wizard with per-step validation and a summary step.

    Chapter 64Validation, Schemas & Form Abstractions

    Advanced Essential 64-validation-and-form-abstractions/

    Opens with: client validation that says "valid", a server that says 400, and a form that shows a generic toast instead of highlighting the bad field. Mental model: 🧠 One schema, two sides: the same schema validates on the client (for experience) and on the server (for safety), and the server always has the final word.

    1. One schema, two sides — sharing schemas between client and server.
    2. Runtime schemas for forms — parsing on submit; coercing form strings.
    3. Server validation errors — mapping API field errors into form errors.
    4. Error typing — field errors, form-level errors, typed error codes.
    5. Form libraries — React Hook Form with a schema resolver; when a library pays off.
    6. React Actions — <form action>, useActionState, useFormStatus, useOptimistic.
    7. Reusable form components — TextField and SelectField bound to typed field names.
    8. Type-safe form abstractions — their limits, and why not to build your own form framework.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Write a schema for the create-task form and infer its type.
    • L2 Application: Map a 400 response's field errors into the form.
    • L3 Challenge: Build <Field name="…"> components that only accept valid field names.
    • L4 Real-world: Rebuild the project wizard with a form library and shared schemas; compare the code size and edge-case handling.

    Chapter 65Authentication & Authorization

    Advanced Essential 65-auth/

    Opens with: a "protected" admin page that anyone can reach by typing the URL, and an API that trusts an isAdmin flag sent by the client. Mental model: 🧠 Authentication answers "who are you?"; authorization answers "what may you do?". The UI can hide things for usability, but only the server can forbid them.

    1. Authentication concepts — sessions vs tokens, cookies, refresh.
    2. Where credentials live — httpOnly cookies vs browser storage, and the security trade-offs.
    3. Auth state as a discriminated union — loading | anonymous | authenticated.
    4. AuthProvider and useAuth — the safe-context pattern from Ch 54, applied.
    5. Protected routes and redirects — including "return to where you were".
    6. Modeling authorization — roles and permissions as literal unions ("task:delete"), derived from a config object (Ch 20) and optionally generated with template literal types (Ch 24); a typed can(user, permission).
    7. 401 and 403 in the API client — refresh flows and forced logout.
    8. UI authorization is not security — enforcing the same rules on the server.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Classify ten checks as authentication or authorization.
    • L2 Application: Implement a typed useAuth() and a RequireAuth route guard.
    • L3 Challenge: Generate a Permission union from a role → permissions config object.
    • L4 Real-world: Add role-based permissions to TaskFlow (owner/admin/member/viewer), enforced in both the UI and the API.

    ✅ Checkpoint — Part X · Building Real Applications

    • Know: feature-based architecture and dependency rules; typed env config; routing with validated params and search params; the five kinds of state; server state vs client state; DTO → domain mapping; response validation; ApiError modeling; every UI state; TanStack Query; typed forms; shared schemas; server error mapping; React Actions; auth and authorization modeling.
    • Build: P13 Typed Forms Kit, P14 TaskFlow Web, P15 Authentication System.
    • Answer:
      1. Why shouldn't components depend on DTO types?
      2. Where should the current filter, the logged-in user, the task list, and a half-typed comment each live? Why?
      3. Show the difference between "what TypeScript believes" and "what the server returned" with code.
      4. Why do you still need server validation if the client validates with the same schema?
      5. Why is UI-only authorization not security?
    • Small challenge: add a "tags" feature end to end (API schema → client → query → form → filter in the URL) in one sitting.
    • Optional project: add real-time updates (server-sent events) to TaskFlow Web with cache updates.
    • Ready signs: you can sketch a feature's layers and types before writing code; external data never reaches components unvalidated.
    • If you struggle, revisit: Ch 32 (runtime safety), Ch 58 (architecture), Ch 60 (state homes), Ch 61 (the boundary).

    🛠 P13 — Typed Forms Kit

    • Difficulty: 🟡 Intermediate · When: Ch 63–64 · Prerequisites: Ch 22, 51, 63–64
    • Concepts used: typed form state, mapped error types, keyof field names, schemas, server error mapping, accessibility.

    🛠 P14 — TaskFlow Web (React + API application)

    • Difficulty: 🟡→🟠 · When: across Part X · Prerequisites: Ch 58–64, P07, P08
    • Concepts used: feature architecture, routing, state architecture, the API boundary, server state, forms, schemas.
    • Requirements:
      1. Pages: projects list, project board, task detail, and settings.
      2. Data from the P07 API through the P08 client and TanStack Query; every response validated.
      3. Filters, sorting, and pagination live in validated search params.

      apps/web/src/

  shared/     # ui/, lib/, config/ (validated env)
