    🛠 P15 — Authentication System

    • Difficulty: 🟠 Advanced · When: Ch 65 · Prerequisites: Ch 65, P07, P14
    • Concepts used: auth flows, httpOnly cookies, discriminated auth state, safe context, route guards, typed permissions, API error handling.
    • Requirements:
      1. Sign-up, sign-in, sign-out, and session persistence (httpOnly cookie sessions on the P07 API).
      2. A password-reset flow with a mocked email transport.
      3. Roles (owner/admin/member/viewer) mapped to a typed permission set, enforced by the API and reflected in the UI.
      4. Protected routes with return-to redirects; global 401 handling; a friendly 403 page.
      5. Rate limiting and lockout on the sign-in endpoint.

    Part XITesting

    Folder: 11-testing/ · Roadmap: Stage 8 — Real Applications · Difficulty: 🟡

    Purpose of the part. Testing was introduced in Ch 19 and Ch 27 for plain TypeScript. This part makes it a professional practice for React applications, starting from the question that organizes everything: what does TypeScript already guarantee, and what must tests prove?

    Chapter 66What TypeScript Catches vs What Tests Catch

    Intermediate Essential 66-types-vs-tests/

    Opens with: a fully typed, zero-error codebase whose "complete task" button marks the wrong task as done. Mental model: 🧠 Layers of safety, each catching a different class of failure:

     Types ............ consistency: shapes, nullability, exhaustiveness, contracts between modules
 Lint ............. suspicious patterns: floating promises, hook rules, unsafe any
 Runtime validation  the outside world: API data, env, storage, input
 Unit tests ....... logic: "given this input, this output"
 Component tests .. behavior from the user's view: "clicking X shows Y"
 Integration tests  features working together, with mocked network
 E2E tests ........ the real app, real browser, critical paths
 Monitoring ....... what actually happens to real users in production
    1. The layered safety model — the diagram above, with a real bug for each layer.
    2. What types prove — and what "it compiles" really means.
    3. What only tests prove — behavior, logic, integration, accessibility.
    4. What only runtime validation proves — external data, again.
    5. Choosing test levels — pyramid vs trophy; confidence per minute of effort.
    6. A test strategy for TaskFlow Web — what to test at each level.
    7. Don't test what the compiler guarantees — redundant tests vs valuable ones.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: For twelve bugs, name the cheapest layer that catches each.
    • L2 Application: Delete five redundant tests from a provided suite (they test what types guarantee).
    • L3 Challenge: Write the bug that every layer except E2E misses.
    • L4 Real-world: Write TaskFlow Web's TESTING.md strategy document.

    Chapter 67Unit Testing Logic, Reducers & Hooks

    Intermediate Essential 67-unit-testing/

    Opens with: a reducer with nine action types and zero tests, and a custom hook that only fails when two timers overlap. Mental model: Pure functions are the easiest things to test, so push logic into them. Hooks are tested by rendering them in a tiny harness.

    1. Testing pure logic — domain functions, mappers, formatters.
    2. Testing reducers — table-driven tests over the action union.
    3. Testing custom hooks — renderHook, act, rerender.
    4. Hooks that need context — typed wrapper providers.
    5. Fake timers and async logic — debounce, retry, polling.
    6. Type-safe mocks — vi.fn<typeof fn>(), vi.mocked, satisfies for fixtures.
    7. Test data factories — buildTask(overrides?: Partial<Task>).
    8. Type tests for app code — locking the public types of hooks and utilities.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Write table-driven tests for a three-action reducer.
    • L2 Application: Test useDebouncedValue with fake timers.
    • L3 Challenge: Build a typed factory library for TaskFlow (buildTask, buildProject, buildUser) with sensible defaults.
    • L4 Real-world: Raise P14's domain and hook coverage to 90% with meaningful tests, not line-chasing.

    Chapter 68Component Testing with Testing Library

    Intermediate Essential 68-component-testing/

    Opens with: a test suite that breaks every time a div becomes a section, because it tested implementation, not behavior. Mental model: 🧠 Test like a user: find things by role and label, interact the way a person would, and assert on what's visible.

    1. Testing like a user — queries by role, label, and text; the query priority.
    2. Rendering with providers — a typed custom render with router, query client, and auth.
    3. User interactions — user-event for typing, clicking, and keyboard.
    4. Async UI — findBy*, waitFor, and avoiding act warnings.
    5. Testing loading and error states — controlling time and data.
    6. Testing forms — validation messages and submission.
    7. Accessibility in tests — roles as an accessibility signal; automated checks.
    8. What not to test — implementation details and snapshot overuse.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Rewrite five fragile queries as role-based ones.
    • L2 Application: Test the create-task form: validation, submission, server error display.
    • L3 Challenge: Test a combobox's keyboard interaction completely.
    • L4 Real-world: Write component tests for every state of the task board (loading/empty/error/ready).

    Chapter 69Integration Testing, API Mocking & E2E

    Advanced Essential 69-integration-and-e2e/

    Opens with: tests that mock fetch with hand-written objects that drifted from the real API months ago. All green, all lying. Mental model: Mock at the network boundary, not inside your code. Keep mocks honest by building them from the same schemas and types as the real API.

    1. Integration tests — testing a whole feature inside the app.
    2. API mocking with MSW — typed handlers using DTO types.
    3. Preventing contract drift — validating fixtures against API schemas; shared fixtures.
    4. Error and edge cases — network failures, 500s, slow responses, empty data.
    5. Testing routing and auth flows — redirects, guards, and expired sessions.
    6. End-to-end tests with Playwright — critical paths, test environments, selectors.
    7. Flaky tests — causes and cures.
    8. Tests in CI — fast feedback, sharding, and artifacts (deepened in Ch 76).

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Write a typed MSW handler for GET /tasks.
    • L2 Application: Test the "complete task" feature end to end with MSW, including rollback on failure.
    • L3 Challenge: Make every MSW fixture fail its test if it stops matching the API schema.
    • L4 Real-world: Write Playwright tests for sign-in → create project → add task → complete task.

    ✅ Checkpoint — Part XI · Testing

    • Know: the layered safety model; test-level trade-offs; unit, hook, component, integration, and E2E testing; typed mocks and factories; network-level mocking; contract drift; flaky-test causes.
    • Build: P16 TaskFlow Web Test Suite.
    • Answer:
      1. Give three bugs TypeScript can't catch and the test level that catches each.
      2. Why prefer role-based queries?
      3. Why mock at the network level instead of mocking your API module?
      4. How do you keep mocks from drifting away from the real API?
      5. When is an E2E test worth its cost?
    • Small challenge: find and fix a flaky test in a provided suite, explaining the root cause.

    🛠 P16 — TaskFlow Web Test Suite

    Part XIIProduction-Ready React

    Folder: 12-production/ · Roadmap: Stage 9 — Production · Difficulty: 🟡→🟠

    Purpose of the part. An app that works on your machine is not an app that works for users. This part covers what changes in production: builds, failures, speed, accessibility, security, visibility, and delivery. It ends the Essential core.

    Chapter 70Production Builds, Bundles & Code Splitting

    Intermediate Essential 70-builds-and-code-splitting/

    Opens with: a 2.4 MB JavaScript bundle, a 6-second first load on a mid-range phone, and a build that passed even though the code had type errors. Mental model: A production build transforms, bundles, and minifies, but it does not type-check. Code splitting means users download only the code for what they're looking at.

    1. What a production build does — transpile, bundle, minify, tree-shake; why the bundler skips type-checking.
    2. Build configuration — modes, env files, tsc -b && vite build.
    3. Source maps in production — debugging without exposing source publicly.
    4. Analyzing bundles — visualizers and dependency cost.
    5. Code splitting — dynamic import(), React.lazy, Suspense.
    6. Route-based splitting and preloading
    7. Bundle considerations — heavy dependencies, icons, polyfills, browser targets.
    8. Deploying a static SPA — hashed assets, caching headers, SPA fallback routing.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Explain why vite build succeeds with type errors, and fix the pipeline.
    • L2 Application: Split TaskFlow Web by route and measure the difference.
    • L3 Challenge: Cut the bundle by 30% by replacing or lazy-loading two dependencies.
    • L4 Real-world: Deploy TaskFlow Web to a static host with correct caching and routing.

    Chapter 71Error Boundaries & Resilient UIs

    Intermediate Essential 71-error-boundaries/

    Opens with: one widget throws on a null field, and the whole dashboard goes blank. Mental model: An error boundary is a try/catch for a subtree's rendering. Place boundaries so a failure takes down the smallest useful piece of UI.

    1. What happens when a component throws — unmounting the tree.
    2. Error boundaries — the one class component you'll still write, and how to type it.
    3. Using a boundary library — typed fallback props and resetting.
    4. Where to place boundaries — app, route, and widget levels.
    5. What boundaries don't catch — event handlers and async code, and how to handle those.
    6. Route-level errors — the router's error elements.
    7. Reporting errors — connecting to monitoring (Ch 75).
    8. Designing fallback UI — retry, degrade gracefully, keep users oriented.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Mark which errors a boundary catches in six snippets.
    • L2 Application: Write a typed ErrorBoundary class with reset support.
    • L3 Challenge: Add widget-level boundaries to P12 with retry.
    • L4 Real-world: Design the error-handling map for TaskFlow Web (which errors, where caught, what users see).

    Chapter 72Rendering Performance

    Advanced Essential 72-rendering-performance/

    Opens with: typing in a filter box lags by 300 ms on a 2,000-row table. Mental model: 🧠 Measure, find the cause, then apply the smallest fix. Most render problems are about state placement, not missing useMemo.

    1. Measuring first — the React Profiler, the browser performance panel, web vitals.
    2. Why components re-render — state, parent renders, context.
    3. Structural fixes — state colocation, splitting components, passing children.
    4. Memoization with evidence — memo, useMemo, useCallback, and the React Compiler in production.
    5. Transitions — useTransition and useDeferredValue for responsiveness.
    6. Virtualizing long lists
    7. Context performance — splitting providers and selecting state.
    8. Performance budgets — making performance a requirement.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Diagnose the cause of re-renders in four Profiler screenshots.
    • L2 Application: Fix the laggy filter with useDeferredValue.
    • L3 Challenge: Virtualize a 10,000-row table while keeping keyboard navigation.
    • L4 Real-world: Set and enforce a performance budget for TaskFlow Web in CI.

    Chapter 73Accessibility

    Intermediate Essential 73-accessibility/

    Opens with: a screen-reader recording of the TaskFlow board: "button, button, button, clickable, clickable". Mental model: Accessibility is correctness for every user. Start with semantic HTML (it's accessible for free), then add keyboard support, focus management, and ARIA only where HTML runs out.

    1. Why accessibility is a requirement — users, legal standards, quality.
    2. Semantic HTML first — buttons, links, landmarks, headings.
    3. Keyboard navigation — focus order and keyboard interactions.
    4. Focus management — modals, route changes, and after actions (refs from Ch 45/53).
    5. ARIA when needed — roles, states, and properties; typed aria-* props.
    6. Accessible forms and errors
    7. Color, motion, and preferences — contrast, prefers-reduced-motion.
    8. Testing accessibility — lint rules, role queries, automated audits, and a manual screen-reader pass.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Replace five div buttons with semantic elements.
    • L2 Application: Make the task board fully keyboard-operable.
    • L3 Challenge: Build an accessible modal: focus trap, Escape, focus return.
    • L4 Real-world: Audit TaskFlow Web against WCAG AA and fix every critical issue.

    Chapter 74Security for Frontend Developers

    Advanced Essential 74-security/

    Opens with: a comment field that renders markdown with dangerouslySetInnerHTML, and a proof-of-concept that steals a token from localStorage. Mental model: 🧠 The browser is enemy territory: anything you ship is public, anything you render may be hostile, and anything the client says must be verified by the server.

    1. The frontend threat model — what attackers can and can't do.
    2. XSS — React's escaping, dangerouslySetInnerHTML, and sanitization.
    3. URL and attribute injection — javascript: URLs and validating hrefs.
    4. Tokens and sessions — storage choices, CSRF, cookie flags.
    5. Secrets and env vars — anything bundled into the browser is public.
    6. Dependency and supply-chain risk — lockfiles, audits, update policies.
    7. Content Security Policy — the basics, and how to roll one out.
    8. Never trust the client — server-side validation and authorization (Ch 32, Ch 65).

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Identify the vulnerability in six snippets.
    • L2 Application: Safely render user-supplied markdown.
    • L3 Challenge: Write a safeHref(url: string) helper with tests covering attack payloads.
    • L4 Real-world: Write a security checklist for TaskFlow Web and add a CSP.

    Chapter 75Observability: Logging, Monitoring & Analytics

    Intermediate Essential 75-observability/

    Opens with: a user reports "the app broke"; there are no logs, no stack traces, and no way to know which version they were on. Mental model: You can't fix what you can't see. Make errors, performance, and product events visible, with typed event definitions so the data stays trustworthy.

    1. Why observability — the feedback loop from production.
    2. Structured logging in the browser — levels, context, and no personal data.
    3. Error tracking — capturing errors with context, release versions, and source maps.
    4. Typed analytics events — a discriminated-union event catalog and a track() function keyed by event name (reuse P05's emitter if you built it).
    5. Performance monitoring — web vitals and real-user monitoring.
    6. Feature flags — typed flag definitions and safe rollouts.
    7. Privacy and consent

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Design the event union for five product events.
    • L2 Application: Report boundary-caught errors with release and route context.
    • L3 Challenge: Make track() reject events whose payloads don't match the catalog, at compile time.
    • L4 Real-world: Build an observability plan for TaskFlow Web: what's logged, tracked, and alerted on.

    Chapter 76CI/CD & Long-Term Maintainability

    Intermediate Essential 76-ci-cd-and-maintainability/

    Opens with: a release that broke production because the type-check step only ran on the author's laptop. Mental model: CI is the team's shared memory of "what must always be true". If it isn't checked automatically, it isn't guaranteed.

    1. A CI pipeline for TypeScript + React — install, type-check, lint, test, build, E2E.
    2. Speed and caching
    3. Preview deployments and required checks
    4. Continuous delivery — environments, promotion, rollback.
    5. Dependency updates — automated update PRs and type-breaking upgrades.
    6. Maintainability practices — strictness ratchets, dead-code detection, type coverage.
    7. Documentation that stays current — READMEs and architecture decision records.
    8. The production checklist — everything in Part XII, in one list.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Order the pipeline steps and justify the order.
    • L2 Application: Write a CI workflow for TaskFlow Web.
    • L3 Challenge: Cut CI time in half with caching and parallelism.
    • L4 Real-world: Run the production checklist against P17 and fix every gap.

    Section 9Advanced & Professional Development

    Book Three — Mastery · Parts XIII–XV · Chapters 77–97

    Everything here builds on the Essential core, and none of it is required to be productive. Each chapter carries a tier label (Advanced or Specialist), and specialist sections inside Advanced chapters are marked ⏭ Safe to skip. Book Three is where the reader learns to design for others, through libraries, design systems, and team-scale architecture, and to recognize when advanced tools are unnecessary.

    Why this material comes after building real apps: variance makes sense once you've been puzzled by a callback-prop error; branded types once you've swapped two IDs; template literal types once you've typed routes and permissions; polymorphic components once you've written five button-link hybrids. Book Three answers questions Book Two made you ask.

    Part XIIIAdvanced TypeScript

    Folder: 13-advanced-typescript/ · Roadmap: Stage 10 — Advanced Types & Patterns · Difficulty: 🟠→🔴

    Purpose of the part. The type system's deep end: compatibility rules and their deliberate holes, nominal patterns in a structural world, and type-level programming. Each chapter separates what an experienced application developer should know (Advanced) from what library and framework authors need (Specialist).

    Chapter Tier Who needs it
    77 Variance & Soundness Advanced Anyone designing callback-heavy APIs
    78 Branded Types Advanced Large apps with many ID and unit types
    79 Advanced Conditional Types Advanced (§5–8 Specialist) Library consumers reading .d.ts; library authors

    Chapter 77Type Compatibility, Variance & Soundness

    Advanced Advanced 77-variance-and-soundness/

    Opens with: a Dog[] passed where an Animal[] is expected, then a Cat pushed into it, with no error. Next to it, a button click handler rejected where an "any element" handler is expected. Why is TypeScript lenient in one case and strict in the other? Mental model: 🧠 Producers are covariant; consumers are contravariant. Things you read from can be narrower (a box of dogs works where a box of animals is read). Things you write to or call must accept at least as much (a handler for any element works where a button handler is needed, but not the reverse).

    1. Assignability revisited — the precise rules behind "fits inside".
    2. Covariance — return types, read-only properties, readonly arrays.
    3. Contravariance — function parameters, and why handlers are checked "backwards".
    4. Bivariance and method shorthand — why methods are exempt from strictFunctionTypes.
    5. Invariance — mutable containers; why Dog[] → Animal[] is technically unsound.
    6. Variance annotations — ⏭ in/out on type parameters, for library authors.
    7. Where TypeScript is unsound on purpose — array covariance, method bivariance, any, assertions, unchecked indexing, optional vs missing properties (exactOptionalPropertyTypes).
    8. Variance in API design — readonly inputs, callback parameter types, safe defaults.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Mark each position in five types as covariant, contravariant, or invariant.
    • L2 Application: Make a function's array parameter readonly and show which unsound calls disappear.
    • L3 Challenge: Write a program that exploits method bivariance to cause a runtime crash, then fix it with function-property syntax.
    • L4 Real-world: Explain (in a PR comment) why a component's onChange type rejects a teammate's handler, and propose the correct type.

    Chapter 78Branded Types & Nominal Typing Patterns

    Advanced Advanced 78-branded-types/

    Opens with: assignTask(projectId, taskId) called as assignTask(taskId, projectId). Both are strings, so it compiles and corrupts data for a week. Mental model: 🧠 A brand is a compile-time tag that makes structurally identical types incompatible. It costs nothing at runtime, and the only way to get one is through a function that checks the value.

    1. When structural identity hurts — IDs, units, validated strings.
    2. Branding with intersections — string & { readonly __brand: "TaskId" }.
    3. Unique-symbol brands — stronger, unforgeable tags.
    4. Smart constructors — brands earned through validation (Ch 32 again); schema-produced brands.
    5. Units and value objects — Meters vs Feet, Money, Email.
    6. Opaque types across modules — hiding construction behind a module boundary.
    7. Brands at the boundary — parse at the edge, carry brands through the app.
    8. When brands are overkill — friction vs the bugs actually prevented.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Define TaskId and ProjectId brands and show that swapping them fails to compile.
    • L2 Application: Add a smart constructor parseEmail(input: string): Result<Email, string>.
    • L3 Challenge: Implement Money with currency safety (adding USD to EUR is a compile error).
    • L4 Real-world: Introduce branded IDs across TaskFlow's API client and frontend; measure the churn and report whether it was worth it.

    Chapter 79Advanced Conditional Types & infer

    Advanced Advanced 79-advanced-conditional-types/

    Opens with: a utility type from a popular library's .d.ts that is twelve lines of nested conditionals. By the end of the chapter, the reader can read it, and write one. Mental model: Conditional types are type-level pattern matching. infer captures, distribution maps over unions, and recursion loops. Together they form a small functional language.

    1. Conditional types through the set model — a recap at full precision.
    2. Controlling distribution — naked vs wrapped type parameters and when each is right.
    3. infer in every position — parameters, returns, constructors, tuple elements, promises, template strings.
    4. infer with constraints — infer U extends string.
    5. Recursive conditional types — ⏭ tail recursion and depth limits.
    6. Generics in implementations — why TypeScript can't narrow T inside a generic function body; overloads vs internal assertions.
    7. Reading library-grade types — decoding a real-world declaration file step by step.
    8. Friendlier type errors — ⏭ making failed constraints readable for your users.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Evaluate eight conditional types, including distribution edge cases.
    • L2 Application: Write FirstParam<F> and LastElement<T> with infer.
    • L3 Challenge: Write IsUnion<T> and explain why it works.
    • L4 Real-world: Document, line by line, the conditional types in a library your project depends on.

    Chapter 80Advanced Mapped & Recursive Types

    Advanced Advanced 80-advanced-mapped-and-recursive-types/

    Opens with: a form library that type-checks register("address.street") and rejects register("address.stret"). How? Mental model: Mapped types transform shapes; recursion lets the transformation descend into nested shapes. Together they can describe every path through an object.

    1. Key remapping in depth — filtering keys by value type (KeysOfType<T, V>).
    2. Mapping over unions of objects — distribution in mapped types.
    3. Recursive types revisited — trees, JSON, nested route configs.
    4. Recursive utility types — DeepPartial, DeepReadonly, DeepRequired, and their edge cases (arrays, functions, dates).
    5. Path types — Paths<T> ("a.b.c") and PathValue<T, P>.
    6. Recursion limits and performance — "type instantiation is excessively deep" and what to do.
    7. When deep types are a smell — flattening data instead of typing depth.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Write DeepReadonly<T> handling arrays.
    • L2 Application: Write KeysOfType<T, V> and use it to type a sortBy that only accepts numeric keys.
    • L3 Challenge: Implement Paths<T> and PathValue<T, P> with type tests.
    • L4 Real-world: Upgrade P13's form kit so field names are typed paths into nested values.

    Chapter 81Template Literal Types in Depth

    Advanced Advanced 81-template-literal-types-in-depth/

    Opens with: navigate("/projects/:projectId/tasks/:taskId", { projectId }), with the missing taskId caught at compile time. Mental model: Template literal types plus infer turn string formats into structured types: the type checker can parse the strings your app relies on.

    1. Review and composition — unions in templates, intrinsic string types.
    2. Parsing strings with infer — ⏭ split, trim, and replace at the type level.
    3. Typed routes — extracting :params from path patterns.
    4. Typed event and message names — namespaces and wildcards (P05, revisited).
    5. CSS and design-token strings — `${number}px`, token paths.
    6. Limits — ⏭ performance, recursion depth, error readability.
    7. When to stop — where a code generator or a plain object map is the better tool.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Write type EventName = `${Entity}:${Action}` for three entities and four actions.
    • L2 Application: Write RouteParams<"/users/:id/posts/:postId"> → { id: string; postId: string }.
    • L3 Challenge: Build a typed href(route, params) helper rejecting missing and extra params.
    • L4 Real-world: Replace TaskFlow Web's route helper (Ch 59) with template-literal-powered types; compare the error messages.

    Chapter 82Advanced Generic Patterns & API Type Design

    Advanced Advanced 82-advanced-generic-patterns/

    Opens with: a query-builder API where where("status", "dun") compiles, because the value type isn't connected to the field. Mental model: The call site is the specification. Design what callers write first, then make inference produce exactly the types that call site needs, and no more.

    1. const type parameters — preserving literal types without as const at call sites.
    2. NoInfer and inference control — choosing which argument "wins" inference.
    3. Builder patterns — types that accumulate through method chains.
    4. Higher-order generics — functions that return generic functions; currying.
    5. Typed factories and dependency injection — typed service containers.
    6. Overloads vs conditional return types — choosing for the caller's experience.
    7. Designing for inference — error ergonomics and discoverability.
    8. Case study: a typed filter/query API — field-aware operators and values.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Use NoInfer to fix a provided inference bug.
    • L2 Application: Write defineRoutes(config) with const type parameters.
    • L3 Challenge: Build a typed createQuery<T>().where(field, op, value) where value's type depends on field and op.
    • L4 Real-world: Design and implement TaskFlow API's typed filter DSL shared by client and server.

    Chapter 83Type-Level Programming & Type-Safe DSLs

    Expert Specialist 83-type-level-programming/

    Opens with: a schema library where you write runtime code, and a fully precise static type appears. Where did it come from? Mental model: The type system is a small, pure, functional programming language that runs inside the compiler, where tuples are lists, conditionals are if, and recursion is the only loop. Treat it like code: name things, test things, and know its costs.

    1. Types as a programming language — conditionals, recursion, tuples as lists.
    2. Tuple manipulation — head, tail, reverse, length.
    3. Type-level arithmetic — ⏭ counting with tuples, and why it's mostly a curiosity.
    4. How schema libraries infer types — building Infer<typeof schema>.
    5. How end-to-end typed APIs work — sharing router types between server and client.
    6. How typed query builders work — inferred result rows from queries.
    7. Designing a small type-safe DSL — a typed config or state-machine DSL.
    8. The cost of cleverness — compile time, error messages, maintainability.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Implement Length<T> and Reverse<T> for tuples.
    • L2 Application: Implement a minimal Infer<Schema> for object and string schemas.
    • L3 Challenge: Type a state-machine DSL where send(event) only accepts events valid in the current state.
    • L4 Real-world: Write a design note on whether a type-level DSL is right for a feature in your capstone, including compile-time measurements.

    ✅ Checkpoint — Part XIII · Advanced TypeScript

    • Know: covariance, contravariance, bivariance, invariance; TypeScript's deliberate unsoundness; branded and opaque types; advanced infer and distribution control; recursive and path types; template literal parsing; const type parameters and NoInfer; builder and DSL patterns; the costs of type-level code.
    • Build: P18 Runtime Validation Library.
    • Answer:
      1. Why are function parameters checked contravariantly, and why are methods an exception?
      2. How do you create a brand that can only be obtained through validation?
      3. What does wrapping a type parameter in [T] change in a conditional type?
      4. How does Paths<T> work, and what are its limits?
      5. When is a type-level DSL the wrong choice?
    • Small challenge: type get(obj, "a.b.c") with a precise return type and a readable error for invalid paths.
    • Optional project: solve ten medium-difficulty type challenges and write explanations, not just solutions.
    • Ready signs: you can read any library's .d.ts and explain it, and you can say no to a clever type.
    • If you struggle, revisit: Ch 22–23 (the foundations of mapped and conditional types), Ch 10 (set model), Ch 77 §1–5.

    🛠 P18 — Runtime Validation Library (a mini-Zod)

    • Difficulty: 🟠→🔴 · When: end of Part XIII · Prerequisites: Ch 32, 78–83
    • Concepts used: generics, mapped types for object shapes, conditional types, infer, branded types, Result<T, E>, type tests.
    • Requirements:
      1. Schema builders: string, number, boolean, literal, object, array, union, optional, nullable, record.
      2. parse (throws) and safeParse (returns Result); errors carry paths such as ["tasks", 3, "title"].
      3. Infer<typeof schema> produces the precise static type, including optional keys.
      4. .refine(predicate, message) and .transform(fn), where transform changes the output type (input and output types are tracked separately).
      5. .brand<"TaskId">() produces branded output types.
      6. Exhaustive type tests and runtime tests; it replaces the schema library in P07 for one module as a proof.
    • Suggested architecture: src/schema.ts (base Schema<Output, Input>), src/primitives/, src/object.ts, src/union.ts, src/errors.ts, src/infer.ts, test/.
    • Stretch goals: implement the Standard Schema interface so other libraries can accept your schemas; discriminated-union fast paths; JSON Schema export.
    • You should understand afterward: how runtime code and static types can be designed together, which is the foundation of modern TypeScript libraries.

    Part XIVAdvanced React + TypeScript Patterns

    Folder: 14-advanced-react-patterns/ · Roadmap: Stage 10 — Advanced Types & Patterns · Difficulty: 🟠

    Purpose of the part. Patterns for building components other developers use: generic, polymorphic, compound, and headless components. Every pattern chapter has two mandatory boxes, and they carry equal weight:

    ✅ When is this useful? · 🚫 When is this unnecessary complexity?

    Each chapter also ends with a de-abstraction exercise: take an over-engineered component and simplify it.

    Chapter 84Advanced Generic Components & Hooks

    Advanced Advanced 84-advanced-generic-components/

    Opens with: the Ch 57 Table<T> grows sorting, filtering, selection, and custom cells, and its column type becomes any "temporarily". Mental model: Column definitions are a typed contract between the row type and the cells: each column's accessor fixes the value type its cell renderer receives.

    1. Generic components, revisited — what changes at library scale.
    2. Typed column definitions — accessor keys (keyof Row) and accessor functions; cells receive the right value type.
    3. Generic hooks for tables — useSort<T>, useFilter<T>, useSelection<T>, usePagination.
    4. Generic components with refs — ref-as-prop in generic components.
    5. Generics and wrappers — preserving generics through memo and other higher-order components.
    6. Controlled and uncontrolled generic components — selected/onSelectedChange vs defaultSelected.
    7. ✅ Useful / 🚫 Unnecessary — generic tables, selects, and lists vs one-off components.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Type a ColumnDef<Row> with key accessors.
    • L2 Application: Add typed sorting where only sortable value types are allowed.
    • L3 Challenge: Support accessor functions with a correctly typed cell value.
    • L4 Real-world (de-abstraction): A generic <Anything<T>> component is used in exactly one place. Inline it and justify the deletion.

    Chapter 85Discriminated & Conditional Props

    Advanced Advanced 85-discriminated-props/

    Opens with: a Button that accepts href and onClick and type="submit" all at once, and nobody knows what happens. Mental model: 🧠 When props depend on each other, the props type is a union of valid configurations. never marks props that are forbidden in a configuration.

    1. Props that depend on each other — recognizing the smell.
    2. Discriminated props — variant unions.
    3. Mutually exclusive props — { href: string; onClick?: never } | { onClick: () => void; href?: never }.
    4. XOR helper types — a reusable XOR<A, B>.
    5. Controlled vs uncontrolled props — typing value + onChange vs defaultValue.
    6. Narrowing destructured props — what works and what loses narrowing.
    7. ✅ Useful / 🚫 Unnecessary — when two components are simpler than one union.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Type an Alert whose onDismiss is required only when dismissible: true.
    • L2 Application: Type an Input that's either controlled or uncontrolled, never both.
    • L3 Challenge: Write XOR<A, B> and use it for three components.
    • L4 Real-world (de-abstraction): Split a five-variant "mega-component" into separate components and compare the call sites.

    Chapter 86Polymorphic Components & the asChild Pattern

    Advanced Advanced 86-polymorphic-components/

    Opens with: Button, LinkButton, RouterLinkButton, and SubmitButton: four copies of the same styles. Mental model: A polymorphic component lets the caller choose the rendered element, and its props type follows that choice. The asChild (slot) pattern avoids most of this type complexity through composition.

    1. The problem — one look, many elements.
    2. The as prop — ElementType and props of the chosen element.
    3. Typing polymorphic props — own props merged with ComponentPropsWithoutRef<C> via Omit.
    4. Refs in polymorphic components — typing the element's ref.
    5. The asChild / Slot pattern — merging props onto the child; much simpler types.
    6. Costs — type-checking speed and error-message quality.
    7. ✅ Useful / 🚫 Unnecessary — design-system primitives vs app components.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Type Text as="h1" | "p" | "span" with a restricted union.
    • L2 Application: Implement a fully polymorphic Box<C>.
    • L3 Challenge: Implement Button asChild with a Slot that merges classes, handlers, and refs.
    • L4 Real-world (de-abstraction): Replace a polymorphic component used in two places with two plain components.

    Chapter 87Compound Components

    Advanced Advanced 87-compound-components/

    Opens with: <Tabs tabs={[{ label, content, disabled, icon, badge }]} />. Every new requirement adds a field to the config object. Mental model: Compound components are a family of components sharing hidden state through context, which gives callers markup-level control while the parent keeps behavior consistent.

    1. The configuration-object problem
    2. Compound components — <Tabs>, <Tabs.List>, <Tabs.Tab>, <Tabs.Panel>.
    3. Shared state via typed context — the safe-context pattern, internal to the family.
    4. Typing the namespace — static properties on function components vs named exports.
    5. Controlled compound components — value / onValueChange.
    6. Accessibility — roles, keyboard support, and ID wiring across children.
    7. ✅ Useful / 🚫 Unnecessary — markup flexibility vs a simple props API.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Build Accordion with Accordion.Item, Accordion.Trigger, and Accordion.Content.
    • L2 Application: Make Tabs controllable and uncontrollable.
    • L3 Challenge: Build an accessible Menu compound component with keyboard navigation.
    • L4 Real-world (de-abstraction): Convert a compound component that's always used the same way back into a single component.

    Chapter 88Render Props, Headless Components & Inversion of Control

    Advanced Advanced 88-render-props-and-headless/

    Opens with: a combobox library whose markup can't be changed, which forces a fork to change one icon. Mental model: Inversion of control means the component provides behavior and the caller provides rendering. Headless components are the extreme: all behavior, zero markup.

    1. Inversion of control — who decides what renders.
    2. Typed render props — render: (state: T) => ReactNode, function-as-children.
    3. Hooks replaced most render props — and where render props still win (virtualization, measured layouts).
    4. Headless components — logic hooks plus caller-owned markup.
    5. Prop getters — getItemProps() returning correctly typed native props.
    6. Slots, revisited — named ReactNode props as lightweight inversion.
    7. ✅ Useful / 🚫 Unnecessary — libraries vs app code.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Convert a render-prop component into a hook.
    • L2 Application: Build a headless useDisclosure with typed prop getters.
    • L3 Challenge: Build a headless useCombobox<T> and two different UIs on top of it.
    • L4 Real-world (de-abstraction): Replace a headless component in app code with a plain component, and document when you'd go back.

    Chapter 89Reusable Component API Design: Choosing the Right Pattern

    Advanced Advanced 89-component-api-design/

    Archetype: Pattern-decision chapter. Opens with: two engineers arguing for compound components vs props for a Card. Both are right in different situations. Mental model: 🧠 The complexity ladder. Start at the bottom and climb only when a real requirement forces you:

     1. Props            <Card title="…" />
 2. Children         <Card>…</Card>
 3. Slots            <Card header={…} footer={…} />
 4. Compound         <Card><Card.Header/>…</Card>
 5. Render props /   <Card renderHeader={(state) => …} /> · useCard()
    headless
 6. Polymorphic      <Card as="article" /> · asChild
    1. The complexity ladder — what each rung buys and costs.
    2. A decision guide — questions that point to the right rung.
    3. Consistency across a component set — naming, variants, sizes, controlled APIs.
    4. Refs, native props, and accessibility — the non-negotiables for reusable components.
    5. Typing variants — variant maps and derived variant prop types.
    6. Documenting component APIs — TSDoc, examples, stories.
    7. De-abstraction — refactoring a component down the ladder.
    8. Principles of type-safe component libraries — a bridge to Ch 93.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Place eight components on the ladder.
    • L2 Application: Write an API review for three P20 components.
    • L3 Challenge: Design a DatePicker API on paper, at two different rungs, with a recommendation.
    • L4 Real-world (de-abstraction): Simplify the most over-engineered component in your codebase.

    ✅ Checkpoint — Part XIV · Advanced React + TypeScript Patterns

    • Know: advanced generic components and typed column definitions; discriminated, exclusive, and controlled/uncontrolled props; polymorphic components and asChild; compound components; render props, headless components, prop getters; the complexity ladder.
    • Build: P19 Generic Data Table, and P20 Component Library (first release).
    • Answer:
      1. When is a polymorphic component worth its type complexity?
      2. Why does asChild usually lead to simpler types than as?
      3. When are compound components better than a props API, and when are they worse?
      4. What problem do headless components solve?
      5. Describe a time you would climb down the complexity ladder.
    • Small challenge: design and implement an accessible, typed Popover compound component in 90 minutes.
    • Optional project: build a headless useCombobox<T> and publish it inside P20.
    • Ready signs: you justify each pattern with a requirement, and you've deleted at least one abstraction.
    • If you struggle, revisit: Ch 50 (props design), Ch 54 (typed context), Ch 57 (generic components), Ch 13 (unions).

    🛠 P19 — Generic Data Table

    • Difficulty: 🟠 Advanced · When: Ch 84 onward · Prerequisites: Ch 57, 84–88
    • Concepts used: generic components and hooks, typed column definitions, headless architecture, controlled/uncontrolled props, virtualization, accessibility.
    • Requirements:
      1. <DataTable<Row>> with typed columns: key or function accessors, with typed cell renderers.
      2. Sorting, per-column filtering (typed by value type), pagination, row selection, and column visibility.
      3. A headless core hook (useDataTable<Row>) and a default UI built on it.
      4. Client-side and server-side modes (server mode integrates with TanStack Query).
      5. Virtualization for 10,000+ rows; full keyboard navigation; correct ARIA grid semantics.
      6. Type tests proving misuse fails (wrong accessor keys, mismatched cell types).
    • Suggested architecture: core/ (state, sorting, filtering, types), react/ (hook + components), stories/, test/.
    • Stretch goals: column resizing and reordering; grouping; typed CSV export.
    • You should understand afterward: generic component design at library quality, and why headless cores make components reusable.

    Part XVProfessional TypeScript & React Engineering

    Folder: 15-professional-engineering/ · Roadmap: Stage 11 — Professional Engineering · Difficulty: 🟠→🔴

    Purpose of the part. Professional TypeScript and professional React are taught together, organized by concern: architecture, public APIs, libraries, design systems, monorepos, compiler performance, frameworks, and teamwork. This is the engineering that happens around code: making it last, scale, and serve other people.

    Concern TypeScript side React side
    Architecture Domain types, layers, boundaries (Ch 90) Feature and state architecture at scale (Ch 90)
    Public APIs Reusable types, generics management (Ch 91) Component APIs (Ch 89 → 93)
    Distribution Library authoring, publishing, semver (Ch 92) Design systems and component libraries (Ch 93)
    Code organization Project references (Ch 94) Shared packages and package boundaries (Ch 94)
    Performance Type-checking performance (Ch 95) Rendering strategy, frameworks (Ch 96)
    People Type conventions and review (Ch 97) Component conventions and review (Ch 97)

    Chapter 90Architecture at Scale: Boundaries, Layers & Domain Modeling

    Advanced Advanced 90-architecture-at-scale/

    Opens with: TaskFlow, two years later: eight teams, 400 components, and a "shared" folder everyone depends on and nobody owns. Mental model: 🧠 Architecture is the set of decisions that are expensive to change. Make boundaries explicit, make dependencies point one way, and let types describe each boundary's contract.

    1. What changes at scale — teams, code volume, lifetimes, coordination cost.
    2. Domain modeling with types — entities, value objects, branded IDs, state machines.
    3. Bounded contexts in a frontend — features as domains with their own language.
    4. Ports and adapters for UI apps — interfaces for API, storage, and analytics; swappable adapters.
    5. State architecture at scale — ownership of state across many features.
    6. Shared types vs coupling — what to share, and what to duplicate deliberately.
    7. Enforcing architecture — lint rules, dependency graphs, package boundaries.
    8. Architecture decision records — capturing why, not only what.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Identify the ports and adapters in TaskFlow Web.
    • L2 Application: Replace direct localStorage usage with a typed Storage port and two adapters.
    • L3 Challenge: Draw TaskFlow's dependency graph and remove one cycle.
    • L4 Real-world: Write three ADRs for your capstone's riskiest decisions.

    Chapter 91Designing Reusable Types & Public APIs

    Advanced Advanced 91-reusable-types-and-public-apis/

    Opens with: a minor release that "only changed types" and broke 40 downstream projects. Mental model: Every exported type is a promise. Make promises you can keep: accept wide inputs, return precise outputs, and hide complexity behind simple names.

    1. Types as API surface — everything exported is a contract.
    2. Inference-first public APIs — callers shouldn't need to write type arguments.
    3. Accept wide, return narrow — readonly inputs, precise outputs.
    4. Managing complex generics — named intermediate types, hiding helpers, simple surfaces.
    5. Avoiding over-engineering — the complexity budget, revisited.
    6. Evolving types safely — @deprecated, overload transitions, additive changes.
    7. Documenting types — TSDoc, examples, and type tests as documentation.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: For eight type changes, decide whether each is breaking.
    • L2 Application: Make a library function's inputs readonly and its outputs more precise without breaking callers.
    • L3 Challenge: Refactor an exported 30-line conditional type into named, documented, tested pieces.
    • L4 Real-world: Write the public-API guidelines for your component library (P20).

    Chapter 92Library Authoring, Publishing & Semantic Versioning

    Expert Advanced 92-library-authoring/

    Opens with: a published package that works in one bundler, fails in Node ESM, and shows any for every import in a CommonJS project. Mental model: 🧠 A package is a contract with every possible consumer environment. exports decides what they can load; declaration files decide what they see; semver decides what they can trust.

    1. Anatomy of a TypeScript package — package.json exports and types conditions.
    2. ESM-first and dual publishing — trade-offs and modern defaults.
    3. Declaration output — declaration, declarationMap, isolatedDeclarations.
    4. Build tools for libraries — bundling vs plain tsc output.
    5. Validating packages — checking type resolution across module modes; package linting.
    6. Semantic versioning for types — what counts as a breaking type change.
    7. API reports and compatibility — tracking public API diffs in CI.
    8. Release automation — changesets, CI publishing, provenance.
    9. Maintaining declarations — ⏭ supporting multiple TypeScript versions.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Write an exports map for a package with ESM, CJS, and types.
    • L2 Application: Publish P04 to a local registry and consume it from ESM and CJS projects.
    • L3 Challenge: Set up an API report that fails CI on unreviewed public API changes.
    • L4 Real-world: Ship a release of P20 with changesets, generated changelog, and validated package types.

    Chapter 93Design Systems & Component Libraries

    Advanced Advanced 93-design-systems/

    Opens with: five slightly different blues, three modal implementations, and a redesign estimated at six months because styles are copy-pasted everywhere. Mental model: A design system is a product for other developers: tokens (decisions), components (implementations), patterns (guidance), and governance (how it evolves).

    1. What a design system is — tokens, components, patterns, governance.
    2. Design tokens as typed data — one source, exported to CSS variables and TypeScript.
    3. Primitives vs composites
    4. Building on accessible headless primitives — buy vs build.
    5. Theming with types — theme contracts and module augmentation.
    6. Documentation — interactive docs with typed stories.
    7. Testing a component library — interaction, accessibility, and visual regression.
    8. Versioning, migration, and adoption — deprecation policy, codemods, measuring adoption.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Split ten style values into tokens and component-specific values.
    • L2 Application: Generate CSS variables and a typed token object from one token file.
    • L3 Challenge: Support light/dark/high-contrast themes with a typed theme contract.
    • L4 Real-world: Write a codemod that migrates <Button kind="…"> to <Button variant="…"> across TaskFlow Web.

    Chapter 94Monorepos & Package Boundaries

    Advanced Advanced 94-monorepos/

    Opens with: the web app and the API each have their own copy of Task, and they've drifted. A field rename shipped to one side only. Mental model: A monorepo makes shared code cheap and boundaries optional, so you must make them explicit. Packages are boundaries with public entry points; project references make TypeScript respect them.

    1. Why monorepos — shared code, atomic changes, consistent tooling.
    2. Workspaces — package-manager workspaces and internal dependencies.
    3. Internal packages — source-shared vs compiled packages.
    4. Project references at scale — composite, tsc -b, incremental builds.
    5. Shared configs — tsconfig, ESLint, and Prettier packages.
    6. Shared contract packages — API schemas and types consumed by both web and api.
    7. Task orchestration and caching — running only what changed.
    8. Enforcing package boundaries — dependency rules and public entry points.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Draw the package graph for the capstone monorepo.
    • L2 Application: Extract TaskFlow's schemas into packages/contracts, used by both apps.
    • L3 Challenge: Configure project references so editing contracts re-checks only dependents.
    • L4 Real-world: Migrate P07 and P14 into one monorepo without breaking CI.

    Chapter 95TypeScript at Scale: Compiler & Type-Checking Performance

    Expert Specialist 95-compiler-performance/

    Opens with: a 90-second type-check, an editor that freezes on hover, and one exported conditional type responsible for half of it. Mental model: Type-checking is computation. Some types are expensive to compute, especially big unions, deep recursion, and complex intersections. Measure before optimizing, just like runtime code.

    1. Where the checker spends time — parsing, binding, checking, instantiation.
    2. Measuring — --extendedDiagnostics and --generateTrace, and reading a trace.
    3. Expensive types — large unions, deep recursion, intersection chains, heavy conditionals.
    4. Cheaper patterns — interfaces over intersections, named types, explicit return annotations.
    5. Project structure for speed — references, incremental builds, skipLibCheck trade-offs.
    6. Editor performance — the language server in large repositories.
    7. The native compiler — what a much faster checker changes, and what it doesn't.
    8. Type performance budgets — tracking check time in CI.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Read an --extendedDiagnostics report and name the top cost.
    • L2 Application: Speed up a provided slow type by restructuring it.
    • L3 Challenge: Use a trace to find the slowest file in a provided repo and fix it.
    • L4 Real-world: Add a type-check time budget to the capstone's CI.

    Chapter 96React Frameworks, Server Rendering & Server Components

    Advanced Advanced 96-frameworks-and-server-components/

    Opens with: TaskFlow's marketing pages need SEO and fast first paint, and the team asks whether to rewrite the SPA "in a framework". Mental model: 🧠 Frameworks move work to the server: rendering (SSR/SSG), data fetching, and with Server Components, entire components. Every server → client crossing is a serialization boundary, which means it is also a trust boundary.

    1. Rendering strategies — client rendering, SSR, SSG, streaming.
    2. Why frameworks — routing, data loading, bundling, and server integration in one model.
    3. Server Components — components that run only on the server.
    4. Client components and the boundary — "use client" and what crosses it.
    5. The serialization boundary — props crossing to the client must be serializable; using types to enforce it.
    6. Server Functions and Actions — typed and validated, because they're public endpoints (Ch 32, once more).
    7. Data fetching on the server — caching and revalidation concepts.
    8. Choosing SPA or framework — the trade-offs, applied to TaskFlow.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Classify ten components as server, client, or either.
    • L2 Application: Build one TaskFlow page with a server component and a client island.
    • L3 Challenge: Write a Server Action with schema validation and typed field errors returned to a form.
    • L4 Real-world: Write a decision record: should TaskFlow Web move to a framework?

    Chapter 97Working on a Team: Code Review, Documentation & Conventions

    Intermediate Essential 97-team-practices/

    Opens with: a 1,200-line PR with a new generic abstraction layer, three as unknown as casts, and the comment "trust me, it's cleaner". Mental model: Code is read by people more than by compilers. Conventions remove decisions, reviews spread knowledge, and simplicity is a feature you defend.

    1. Reviewing TypeScript + React code — a practical checklist.
    2. Type smells in review — any, as, !, non-exhaustive switches, lying generics, fake context defaults.
    3. Reviewing for simplicity — challenging unnecessary abstraction kindly.
    4. Team conventions — naming, file structure, and lint rules as executable conventions.
    5. Documentation — READMEs, ADRs, TSDoc, onboarding guides.
    6. Trade-offs as team decisions — performance vs complexity, safety vs speed.
    7. Maintaining large codebases — strictness ratchets, codemods, deprecations, upgrade playbooks.
    8. Growing as an engineer — mentoring, writing, and teaching what you know.

    This chapter is Essential despite its position. Any developer on a team needs it, and readers on the fast-track path read it right after Part XII.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Find every type smell in a provided diff.
    • L2 Application: Write review comments for a PR that are specific, kind, and actionable.
    • L3 Challenge: Turn three of your team's unwritten rules into lint rules or config.
    • L4 Real-world: Write the CONTRIBUTING.md and an onboarding guide for your capstone repository.

    ✅ Checkpoint — Part XV · Professional Engineering

    • Know: domain modeling and boundaries at scale; ports and adapters; public type design and evolution; package anatomy, exports, declaration output, type-level semver, release automation; design-system structure and theming; monorepo workspaces, references, shared contracts; type-check performance; rendering strategies and Server Components; review and conventions.
    • Build: P20 Component Library (published), and the capstone architecture (Ch 98).
    • Answer:
      1. What makes a type change breaking? Give three examples.
      2. Why should a shared contracts package exist, and what should not go in it?
      3. How do you find out why type-checking is slow?
      4. What crosses the server/client boundary in Server Components, and why is it a trust boundary?
      5. What's on your code-review checklist for TypeScript + React?
    • Small challenge: review a provided PR and write the review as you would at work.
    • Optional project: contribute a typed fix or documentation improvement to an open-source TypeScript project.
    • Ready signs: you can explain and defend the architecture of a codebase, including what you chose not to build.
    • If you struggle, revisit: Ch 58 (app architecture), Ch 89 (component API design), Ch 91 (public types), Ch 94 (package boundaries).

    🛠 P20 — Reusable Component Library (@taskflow/ui)

    • Difficulty: 🟠 Advanced · When: starts in Part XIV, published in Part XV · Prerequisites: Ch 84–89, 91–94
    • Concepts used: component API design, polymorphism/asChild, compound components, headless hooks, typed tokens and themes, accessibility, library packaging, semver, documentation, testing.
    • Requirements:
      1. Tokens package (typed source → CSS variables) and themes (light/dark) with a typed theme contract.
      2. Components: Button (asChild), TextField, Select<T>, Dialog (compound), Tabs (compound), Tooltip, Toast (context API), and the P19 DataTable.
      3. Every component: native props extension, ref support, keyboard and screen-reader support, TSDoc, stories.
      4. Interaction, accessibility, and visual-regression tests.
      5. Published (local registry or npm) with an exports map, validated types, changesets, and a changelog.
      6. Consumed by TaskFlow Web inside the monorepo.
    • Suggested architecture:
      packages/
  tokens/        # source of truth → css vars + typed tokens
  ui/            # components (src/<component>/), index.ts public API
  ui-docs/       # interactive documentation site
    • Stretch goals: a codemod for one deliberate breaking change; server-component-compatible entry points ("use client" boundaries); a theme builder.
    • You should understand afterward: what it takes to build software for other developers, and how types, docs, tests, and versioning make that trustworthy.

    P15 Authentication System X Advanced 🟠 Auth flows, typed permissions, server enforcement C1
    P17 Complex Dashboard (Production) XII Advanced 🟠 Performance, resilience, a11y, security, observability C2

    C2 Ledgerly (frontend-focused) XVI Professional 🟠→🔴 Everything except the backend chapters —
    C3 Library track XVI Professional / Specialist 🔴 Book Three in depth —

    The project levels follow the brief's categories. Beginner: calculator, todo, utilities, basic components. Intermediate: generic library, dashboard, API client, forms, Node API, React + API app. Advanced: validation system, event emitter, data table, component library, auth, complex dashboard. Professional: the capstones.

    Part XVICapstone

    Folder: 16-capstone/ · Roadmap: Stage 12 — Capstone · Difficulty: 🟠→🔴

    Purpose of the part. Two chapters guide the capstone from requirements to a reviewed, shipped system. The book's voice changes from teacher to senior colleague: it asks questions, gives checklists, and reviews decisions, but no longer gives instructions step by step.

    Chapter 98Capstone Planning: From Requirements to Architecture

    Advanced Essential 98-capstone-planning/

    Opens with: a one-paragraph product brief, deliberately vague, from a fictional product manager. Mental model: Design from the inside out: domain types first, then contracts, then architecture, then UI. Types are the cheapest place to discover a bad design.

    1. Choosing your track — C1, C2, or C3, based on your goals and reading path.
    2. From brief to user stories — acceptance criteria, scope, non-goals.
    3. Modeling the domain in types — entities, states, transitions, branded IDs, before any UI.
    4. Designing the API contract — schemas as the shared source of truth.
    5. Architecture and package boundaries — the monorepo layout and dependency rules.
    6. Planning state, data, and errors — the state map, the error contract, and the UI-states inventory.
    7. Quality strategy — test plan, accessibility targets, performance and type-check budgets, security checklist.
    8. Milestones and scope control — a walking skeleton first; cutting scope without cutting quality.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Turn the brief into ten user stories with acceptance criteria.
    • L2 Application: Write the domain types and state machines; review them against the stories.
    • L3 Challenge: Write the contract package (schemas + inferred types) before any implementation.
    • L4 Real-world: Produce the capstone design document: domain, contract, architecture diagram, state map, quality plan, milestones, and three ADRs.

    Chapter 99Building, Shipping & Reviewing Your Capstone

    Expert Essential 99-capstone-build-and-review/

    Opens with: "Deploy something on day one." A walking skeleton that does almost nothing, all the way to production. Mental model: Ship thin vertical slices. Each slice crosses every layer (contract, API, client, UI, tests) and leaves the system deployable.

    1. The walking skeleton — CI, deploy, env validation, and one end-to-end request.
    2. Building feature slices end to end — contract → API → client → UI → tests.
    3. Hardening — error paths, edge cases, security review.
    4. Performance and accessibility passes — measured against your budgets.
    5. Observability and operations — error tracking, analytics events, runbooks.
    6. Documentation and the architecture review — README, ADRs, contributing guide.
    7. Self-review against the rubric — §10.6, scored honestly.
    8. Presenting your work — demo, write-up, portfolio.
    9. What's next — where to go after the book.

    Exercises:

    • L1 Recall: Write the definition of done for one feature slice.
    • L2 Application: Ship the walking skeleton with CI and a deployed preview.
    • L3 Challenge: Run a full self-review against the rubric and fix the three weakest areas.
    • L4 Real-world: Get a code review from another developer, address it, and write a short retrospective.

    10.2 Capstone C1 — Teamboard (full-stack, recommended)

    A multi-tenant project and issue tracker for small teams: the TaskFlow thread at professional scale.

    • Difficulty: 🔴 Expert / Professional
    • Prerequisites: Essential core (Parts I–XII) + Ch 90–94 + Ch 97 (recommended: Ch 78, 84–89)
    • Concepts used: domain modeling, branded IDs, discriminated unions and state machines, schemas as contracts, layered Node API, repository pattern, runtime validation at every boundary, typed env, auth sessions and typed permissions, feature-based React architecture, routing with validated search params, server state, forms with shared schemas, generic data table, component library, error boundaries, performance, accessibility, security, observability, testing at all levels, monorepo, CI/CD.

    Functional requirements

    1. Workspaces: create a workspace; invite members by email (mock transport); roles: owner/admin/member/guest.
    2. Projects and issues: an issue lifecycle modeled as a state machine (backlog → todo → in_progress → in_review → done, plus cancelled) with per-state data (e.g., in_review requires a reviewer).
    3. Board and list views: drag between columns; a list view using the P19 data table with sorting, filtering, and saved views.
    4. Filters in the URL: shareable, validated, with sensible defaults.
    5. Comments: markdown (sanitized), @mentions, and edit history.
    6. Activity feed and notifications: in-app notifications; real-time updates via server-sent events or WebSockets.
    7. Attachments: validated file type and size, stored with metadata.
    8. Dashboards: throughput, cycle time, and workload charts (from P17).
    9. Permissions: enforced by the API, reflected in the UI, with typed can(user, permission).
    10. Audit log for permission-sensitive actions.

    Non-functional requirements

    • Every network, storage, env, file, and URL boundary is validated, and as appears only in a documented allowlist.
    • No any in application code (lint-enforced); exhaustive handling of every union.
    • Tests: domain ≥ 90%, every feature has integration tests, four E2E critical paths.
    • WCAG AA, keyboard-complete board.
    • Performance budgets: initial JS budget, interaction latency, type-check time.
    • A security checklist completed, CSP enabled, httpOnly sessions, rate-limited auth.
    • Error tracking with source maps; a typed analytics event catalog.
    • CI: type-check, lint, unit/component/integration tests, build, E2E, preview deploy.

    Suggested architecture

    teamboard/
├── apps/
│   ├── web/                  # React SPA (feature-based: features/{issues,projects,workspaces,auth,…})
│   └── api/                  # Node API (config, http, services, repositories, domain, errors)
├── packages/
│   ├── contracts/            # schemas + inferred types + error contract (single source of truth)
│   ├── domain/               # pure domain logic shared by api and web (state machines, rules)
│   ├── ui/                   # component library (P20)
│   ├── tokens/               # design tokens
│   └── config/               # shared tsconfig / eslint / prettier
├── e2e/                      # Playwright
├── docs/adr/                 # architecture decision records
└── .github/workflows/        # CI/CD

    Milestones: M1 walking skeleton → M2 auth and workspaces → M3 projects and issues (API + list) → M4 board and state machine → M5 comments, activity, and real-time → M6 dashboards → M7 hardening (security, a11y, performance) → M8 docs, review, and presentation.

    Stretch goals: offline support with a sync queue; a public REST API with generated client SDK; an end-to-end typed RPC layer as an alternative to REST; a server-rendered marketing site using a framework (Ch 96); internationalization.

    You should understand afterward: how every concept in the book contributes to a real system, and how to defend the system's design to a senior engineer.

    10.3 Capstone C2 — Ledgerly (frontend-focused)

    A personal-finance analytics app. Ideal for readers on the fast-track path or who skipped the backend chapters.

    • Difficulty: 🟠→🔴
    • Prerequisites: Essential core (Parts I–XII; Part VI optional), recommended Ch 78 and 84
    • Concepts used: branded Money and multi-currency safety, CSV parsing pipelines with Result types, rule DSL typing, runtime validation at file/storage/API boundaries, generic data table, typed forms, state architecture, offline storage, charts, performance, accessibility, testing with MSW.

    Functional requirements

    1. Import bank transactions from CSV with column mapping; every row is parsed, and failures are reported per row (no silent drops).
    2. Categorize with user-defined rules (a small typed rule DSL: field, operator, value), plus manual overrides.
    3. Budgets per category with progress, alerts, and rollover.
    4. Recurring payment detection and an upcoming-bills view.
    5. Multi-currency with branded Money (adding different currencies is a compile error) and exchange rates from a public API, validated and cached.
    6. Analytics: spending over time, category breakdown, net worth; a 50,000-row virtualized transaction table.
    7. Offline-first: data stored in IndexedDB (a validated storage boundary), with import/export backups.
    8. Mocked backend for sync, via MSW, for multi-device simulation.

    Non-functional requirements: as C1 for types, tests, accessibility, performance, and security. In addition, the CSV import pipeline must have property-based or table-driven tests for malformed input.

    Suggested architecture

    ledgerly/
├── src/
│   ├── app/                  # router, providers, layout
│   ├── features/{import,transactions,budgets,rules,analytics,settings}/
│   ├── domain/               # Money, Currency, Transaction, Rule DSL (pure, heavily tested)
│   ├── boundaries/           # csv/, storage/ (IndexedDB), rates-api/ — all parse unknown → domain
│   └── shared/{ui,hooks,lib,observability}/
├── mocks/                    # MSW handlers built from schemas
└── e2e/

    Milestones: M1 skeleton + storage boundary → M2 CSV import pipeline → M3 transactions table → M4 rules engine → M5 budgets → M6 multi-currency → M7 analytics → M8 hardening, docs, and review.

    Stretch goals: installable progressive web app; web worker for analytics; encrypted backups; a plugin system for importers (typed plugin contract).

    You should understand afterward: how far careful types and boundary design can take a frontend-only application, and how to keep complex client-side logic correct.

    10.4 Capstone C3 — Library track (Specialist)

    Publish and maintain a TypeScript library used by a real consumer. For readers heading toward library, platform, or tooling work.

    • Difficulty: 🔴 Expert / Specialist
    • Prerequisites: Parts XIII–XV (all), P18 or P20
    • Choose one:
      • (a) P18 grown into a production validation library;
      • (b) P20 grown into a public design system;
      • (c) a typed SDK generator: given a contract definition, generate a fully typed client.
    • Concepts used: type-level programming, inference-first API design, declaration output, exports maps, dual-module publishing, type tests, API reports, semver for types, release automation, compiler performance, documentation.

    Requirements

    1. A documentation site with guides, API reference, and runnable examples.
    2. Runtime tests, type tests, and (for UI) interaction, accessibility, and visual tests.
    3. Package validation in CI for every supported module mode; an API report checked on every PR.
    4. Changesets-driven releases with changelogs and provenance.
    5. Benchmarks, plus type-check performance measurements for large inputs.
    6. One deliberate breaking change shipped with a migration guide (and a codemod for UI libraries).
    7. A real consumer: Teamboard, Ledgerly, or TaskFlow uses the library from the registry, not from source.
    8. CONTRIBUTING.md, issue templates, and a support policy for TypeScript versions.

    Suggested architecture

    your-library/
├── packages/core/       # the library
├── packages/<adapters>/ # optional integrations (e.g., react bindings)
├── docs/                # documentation site
├── bench/               # runtime + type-check benchmarks
├── examples/            # consumer apps (ESM, CJS, bundler)
└── .changeset/

    Stretch goals: implement an interoperability standard (e.g., the Standard Schema interface for a validation library); support multiple TypeScript versions; build an ESLint plugin that accompanies the library.

    You should understand afterward: the full lifecycle of software built for other developers: design, types, documentation, compatibility, and maintenance.

    10.5 Capstone milestones and review cadence

    Milestone Deliverable Review question
    Design Design doc, domain types, contract, ADRs "Could someone build this from your types alone?"
    Skeleton Deployed end-to-end request with CI "Is every quality gate automated from day one?"
    Each slice Contract → API → UI → tests "Is every UI state handled? Is every boundary parsed?"
    Hardening Security, a11y, performance passes "What breaks first under hostile input, slow networks, or a screen reader?"
    Final Docs, demo, rubric self-score "What did you choose not to build, and why?"

    10.6 Capstone evaluation rubric

    Score each dimension 1–4. A professional-quality capstone scores 3+ in every dimension.

    Dimension 1 — Emerging 2 — Developing 3 — Professional 4 — Exemplary
    Domain types Loose objects, booleans Some unions Illegal states unrepresentable; branded IDs Types read as the domain's documentation
    Boundaries as on external data Some validation Every boundary parsed; one source of truth Contracts shared, drift-proof, tested
    Architecture Flat, tangled Folders by type Features + layers + enforced rules Ports/adapters, ADRs, clean package graph
    React design Prop drilling, effect soup Mostly correct state homes Correct state homes, minimal effects, typed APIs Reusable patterns used only where justified
    UI states Happy path only Loading and error Loading, empty, error, partial, success everywhere Graceful degradation and recovery
    Testing Few tests Unit tests only Unit + component + integration + E2E paths Contract tests; no flaky tests; fast CI
    Accessibility Mouse-only Semantic HTML WCAG AA, keyboard-complete Screen-reader tested, focus choreography
    Performance Unmeasured Measured Budgets met and enforced in CI Profiling-driven optimizations documented
    Security Unconsidered Basic escaping Checklist complete, CSP, safe sessions Threat model documented
    Operability Console logs Error tracking Tracking + typed analytics + runbook Dashboards and alerts on real signals
    Simplicity Over- or under-engineered Inconsistent Abstractions justified Documented "not built" decisions
    Documentation None README README, ADRs, CONTRIBUTING New developer productive in an hour

    ✅ Checkpoint — Part XVI · The Journey

    • Know: how every part of the book fits into one system.
    • Build: one capstone (C1, C2, or C3) scoring 3+ in every rubric dimension.
    • Answer:
      1. Walk through one feature from domain type to deployed UI, naming every boundary.
      2. Which three design decisions would you defend in an interview, and which one would you change?
      3. What did TypeScript catch in your capstone that tests wouldn't have, and the reverse?
      4. What did you choose not to abstract?
    • Small challenge: onboard another developer onto your capstone using only its documentation.
    • Ready signs: you can take a vague requirement to production on your own, and explain every choice.
    • If you struggle, revisit: the rubric's lowest dimension maps directly back to a part: types → III–IV, boundaries → VI and Ch 61, architecture → Ch 58 and 90, React → VIII–IX, testing → XI, production → XII, simplicity → Ch 89 and 97.

    Section 12Complete Lessons Folder Structure

    The repository is the book in source form: every part, chapter, and section has a folder, so the codebase can grow into the published e-book without restructuring. The trees in §12.3–12.5 are generated from the chapter cards, so they always match the curriculum.

    On this page
    • 12.1 Design principles
    • 12.2 Folder anatomy
    • A part folder
    • A chapter folder
    • A lesson folder
    • A project folder
    • Naming conventions
    • 12.3 Complete tree: parts and chapters
    • 12.4 Complete tree: every lesson folder
    • 12.5 Projects folder
    • 12.6 Root, shared, and tooling folders
    • 12.7 How the repository becomes the e-book

    12.1 Design principles

    1. The folder hierarchy mirrors the book. Part → Chapter → Lesson (= section). Nobody has to translate between "where am I in the book" and "where am I in the repo".
    2. Numbers carry order; names carry meaning. Parts are 01–16, chapters are numbered globally 01–99 (matching the book), and lessons restart at 01 inside each chapter.
    3. Every lesson is runnable. Examples run with one command; exercises have tests that check them automatically (including type tests).
    4. Solutions are separated. They mirror the tree but live on a separate branch (or a solutions/ tree excluded from the default view), so learners must opt in.
    5. Projects live outside chapters. Projects span several chapters, so they get their own projects/ tree, and chapters link to them.
    6. One workspace. A single pnpm workspace with shared configs means pnpm test works from anywhere, and each lesson needs no setup of its own.

    12.2 Folder anatomy

    A part folder

    08-thinking-in-react/
├── README.md              # Part intro: purpose, roadmap stage, chapter list, prerequisites
├── checkpoint/
│   ├── README.md          # Know · Build · Answer · Challenge · Ready signs · Revisit-if
│   ├── questions.md       # self-assessment questions (answers in solutions/)
│   └── challenge/         # the timed small challenge (starter + tests)
└── 37-react-mental-model/ … 48-custom-hooks/

    A chapter folder

    16-why-generics/
├── README.md              # Chapter text: opening problem, mental model, connections,
│                          #   summary, key takeaways, what comes next
├── 01-the-duplication-problem/      # one folder per section (= lesson)
├── 02-youve-used-generics-already/
├── …
└── exercises/
    ├── l1-recall/         # each: README.md (task) · starter/ · tests/ (runtime + type tests)
    ├── l2-application/
    ├── l3-challenge/      # hints folded inside README
    └── l4-real-world/     # ticket-style brief with acceptance criteria

    A lesson folder

    03-type-parameters/
├── README.md              # The section text (book prose, ≤ ~1,500 words)
├── examples/
│   ├── 01-tiny.ts         # rung 1: one idea, 3–10 lines
│   ├── 02-larger.ts       # rung 2: combined with one earlier idea
│   └── 03-realistic.ts    # rung 3: recognizable app code (rung 4 lives in projects/)
└── exercises/
    ├── 01-predict-the-type.ts       # quick L1/L2 drills for this lesson
    └── 01-predict-the-type.test.ts

    React lessons use .tsx and include a tiny Vite entry so examples run in the browser.

    A project folder

    projects/p07-taskflow-api/
├── README.md              # Prerequisites · Difficulty · Concepts · Requirements ·
│                          #   Architecture · Stretch goals · What you should understand
├── starter/               # skeleton with tests for acceptance criteria
├── milestones/            # v1 (Ch 31), v2 (Ch 32–33): briefs + checkpoint tests
└── REVIEW.md              # self-review checklist

    Naming conventions

    Thing Pattern Example
    Part NN-kebab-title 04-generics-and-type-transformations
    Chapter NN-kebab-short-title (global number) 17-generic-functions-and-constraints
    Lesson NN-kebab-section-title (local number) 04-keyof-with-generics
    Exercise l1-recall … l4-real-world l3-challenge
    Project pNN-kebab-name, capstones/cN-name p19-generic-data-table
    Example file NN-rung.ts(x) 02-larger.ts
