    12.6 Root, shared, and tooling folders

    typescript-react-book/
├── package.json               # workspace scripts: test, typecheck, lint, check:exercise <path>
├── pnpm-workspace.yaml        # projects/*, projects/capstones/*, shared/* (lessons run from the root package)
├── tsconfig.base.json         # strict + noUncheckedIndexedAccess + verbatimModuleSyntax
├── eslint.config.js           # typescript-eslint (type-aware) + react-hooks + jsx-a11y
├── vitest.workspace.ts        # one runner for all lessons and projects
├── shared/
│   ├── tsconfig/              # node.json · react.json · library.json (Ch 26 templates)
│   ├── test-utils/            # typed custom render, MSW server, factories (Part XI)
│   └── fixtures/              # schema-validated sample data (TaskFlow, dashboards)
├── appendices/                # A–H (see the table of contents)
├── front-matter/              # preface, how-to-read, reading paths, setup
├── solutions/                 # mirrors parts/ and projects/; separate branch recommended
└── tools/
    ├── scaffold.ts            # creates part/chapter/lesson folders from the curriculum
    ├── check-exercise.ts      # runs one exercise's runtime + type tests with friendly output
    ├── build-book.ts          # concatenates READMEs in order → e-book (EPUB/PDF/web)
    └── lint-links.ts          # verifies cross-chapter links ("🔗 Ch 32") resolve

    12.7 How the repository becomes the e-book

    lesson README.md files ──┐
chapter README.md files ─┼──► tools/build-book.ts ──► ordered manuscript ──► web book / EPUB / PDF
part README.md files ────┘        (numbering, callout styling, cross-links, code from examples/)
examples/*.ts ───────────────► embedded into the manuscript by reference, so code in the book is
                               always the code that compiles and passes tests in CI

    Why this matters: every code sample in the published book is type-checked and tested on every commit, so the book can't ship a snippet that doesn't compile.

    13.6 Where roadmap and book intentionally differ

    Difference Reason
    Stage 4 spans two parts (V and VI) Toolchain chapters (settings, tools) and boundary chapters (concepts, architecture) need different chapter archetypes, even though they're learned together.
    Stage 8 spans two parts (X and XI) Testing is learned alongside app-building, but gets its own part so it is never buried or skipped.
    Stage 10 spans two parts (XIII and XIV) Type-level skills and component patterns are learned together, but taught separately so each can be skipped independently.
    The JavaScript checkpoint is a chapter (Ch 4), not a stage of its own It's a readiness gate, not new learning.
    Ch 97 (team practices) is Essential but sits in Book Three It reads best after real projects. Fast-track readers are routed to it directly after Part XII.
    Projects don't map 1:1 to parts Projects span chapters (P07 grows across Ch 31–33; P20 across Parts XIV–XV), so they live in projects/, not in chapter folders.

    14.1 Distribution

    Difficulty Chapters Share Where they cluster
    🟢 Beginner 16 16% Parts I–II, the start of Parts VII–VIII

    14.2 The shape of the curve: a sawtooth, not a ramp

    The curve is deliberately a sawtooth. Each new domain (the language, React, mastery) restarts at a gentler slope, so the learner's confidence resets upward even as their skill keeps climbing.

    Average chapter difficulty per part        1 = 🟢   2 = 🟡   3 = 🟠   4 = 🔴
                                           |         |         |         |
BOOK ONE    Part I     Why TypeScript?     █                                  1.0
            Part II    Foundations         █                                  1.0
            Part III   Thinking in Types   ███████████                        2.0
            Part IV    Generics & Types    ███████████████                    2.4
            Part V     Toolchain           ███████████                        2.0
            Part VI    Server & Boundaries ████████████████                   2.5
BOOK TWO    Part VII   To Interfaces       ████                               1.3  ◄ new domain:
            Part VIII  Thinking in React   ███████                            1.6    the slope restarts
            Part IX    React + TS          ████████████                       2.1
            Part X     Real Applications   ████████████████                   2.5
            Part XI    Testing             ██████████████                     2.3
            Part XII   Production          ██████████████                     2.3
BOOK THREE  Part XIII  Advanced TS         ██████████████████████             3.1  ◄ mastery
            Part XIV   Advanced Patterns   █████████████████████              3.0
            Part XV    Professional        ██████████████████████             3.1
            Part XVI   Capstone            ██████████████████████████         3.5

    Why the dip at Parts VII–VIII is intentional: learning React's model is a new kind of thinking (rendering, snapshots, synchronization). Combining it with hard TypeScript at the same time overloads learners, so Part VIII keeps types simple on purpose and Part IX brings the TypeScript difficulty back.

    14.3 The biggest conceptual jumps

    These are the eight places where learners most often stall. Each has dedicated preparation and extra support built in.

    # Jump Why it's hard Preparation before it Extra support at it
    1 Ch 10: types as sets Moves from "labels on values" to reasoning about relationships between types Ch 6–9 build intuition with concrete types Set-diagram drills; 20 assignability predictions; the model is reused in every later part
    2 Ch 13–14: discriminated unions + narrowing Requires modeling states, not just shapes Ch 8 literal types; Ch 9 never "Boolean soup" refactor kata; predict-the-narrowed-type drills; P02 is built around it
    3 Ch 16–18: generics Abstracting over types is a new level of abstraction P03 deliberately creates the duplication pain; Ch 7 introduces Array<T> syntax Six-chapter slow ramp; "predict T" drills; golden-rule checklist
    4 Ch 22–23: mapped and conditional types Programming with types; distributivity surprises Ch 21 uses utility types as black boxes first Rebuild-the-built-in exercises; evaluate-by-hand worksheets
    5 Ch 32: runtime safety Unlearning "types protect me"; a design shift to boundaries Ch 3 (erasure), Ch 9 (unknown), Ch 14 (guards), Ch 31 (built naively on purpose) Break-your-own-API exercise; boundary-mapping diagrams
    6 Ch 41 + 44: snapshots and effects Stale closures and synchronization defy imperative intuition Ch 4 closures self-check; Ch 37 render model; Ch 43 hooks model Render-timeline diagrams; "event or effect?" classification drills
    7 Ch 61–62: the network boundary and server state Two ideas at once: untrusted data and caching Ch 32–33, P08, Ch 60 (state kinds) Hand-rolled useQuery first, so the library solves felt problems
    8 Ch 77 + 83: variance and type-level programming Formal reasoning; recursion at the type level Ch 10, 22–24, and real callback-prop puzzles from Book Two Explicit Specialist fencing; "when to stop" sections

    14.4 Where learners are likely to struggle (and the built-in mitigation)

    Struggle Typical symptom Mitigation
    Reading compiler errors "The error makes no sense", so they reach for as Ch 5 §6 teaches error anatomy; Appendix C decodes the 40 most common errors; every ⚠️ box quotes real errors
    The as habit Assertions used to silence errors Ch 10 §7 frames as as a promise; Ch 32 shows the cost; Ch 97 makes it a review smell
    tsconfig and module resolution Import errors, "works in tsx, fails in tsc" Ch 5 starter config with forward references; Ch 25–26 teach by before/after output
    Over-annotation, or under-annotation Redundant types, or any leaking Ch 6 "annotate boundaries" rule, repeated in Ch 50 and 91
    Generic inference Explicit type arguments everywhere Ch 16 §4, Ch 18 §6, the golden rule, and "no angle brackets at call sites" test rules in P04
    Effect dependencies Infinite loops; lint suppression Ch 44 §3 and §7; the "you might not need an effect" decision table
    Keys and state identity State jumps between list items Ch 40's reproduce-the-bug exercise
    Context defaults Crashes outside providers Ch 54's safe-context pattern, reused in Ch 65 and 87
    Async tests Flaky tests, act warnings Ch 68 §4 and Ch 69 §7
    Architecture paralysis "Where does this file go?" Ch 58's feature template; P14's prescribed structure

    16–17 Generics 25 "predict T" drills; 10 constraint-design problems

    14.7 What can safely be skipped initially

    Skip for now Come back when…
    Ch 23–24 (conditional, template literal, custom utility types) You need to read complex library types, or before Part XIII
    Ch 29 (JS → TS migration) and P06 You join a mixed JS/TS codebase
    Ch 15 §12 (decorators) You work with a decorator-based framework
    Ch 77 §6, 79 §5 and §8, 81 §2 and §6, 83 (all) You author libraries or type-level tooling
    Part XIII (all) Advanced types start appearing in your code reviews
    Part XIV (all) You build shared components for other teams
    Ch 90–96 You work on a large codebase, a library, a monorepo, or a framework-based app
    Ch 95 (compiler performance) Type-checking takes more than about 30 seconds
    Capstone C3 You want to pursue library or platform work

    Never skip: the checkpoints, Ch 10, Ch 13–14, Ch 16–17, Ch 32, Ch 41–44, Ch 52, Ch 61, and Ch 97.

    14.8 Pacing guidance

    • After each 🟠 cluster (Part IV's second half, Ch 32–33, Ch 61–65), schedule a consolidation week: no new chapters, only the part's project.
    • Chapters marked 🔴 should be read twice: once for the shape of the ideas, and again with the exercises.
    • If a checkpoint takes more than twice the expected time, follow its revisit list before continuing.

    Section 15Essential vs Advanced vs Specialist

    Essential: every TypeScript + React developer should know it. Advanced: important for experienced developers and larger applications. Specialist: for library authors, framework developers, type-system enthusiasts, or highly advanced engineers.

    The rule this book follows: nothing Specialist is a prerequisite for anything Essential. A reader who masters only the Essential tier is a productive professional.

    15.3 How the book keeps Specialist knowledge from feeling mandatory

    1. Tier badges on every chapter, explained in the front matter, plus ⏭ fences on Specialist sections inside other chapters.
    2. Book Three framing: "Everything here is optional for being productive."
    3. Reading path B (fast track) is defined as "the Essential tier", and the book explicitly says that finishing it means you're job-ready.
    4. Checkpoints mark optional questions for Advanced chapters (e.g., the Part IV and Part V fast-track notes).
    5. No Essential chapter depends on a Specialist one. This is checked as part of the curriculum review (Section 16): every forward reference from Essential material points to an Essential chapter or is marked "optional".
    6. "When not to" sections in every Advanced chapter normalize not using the feature.

    16.1 How the review was done

    Three passes over the complete curriculum:

    1. Sequencing pass. For every chapter: is each concept it uses taught earlier, or explicitly previewed? (This produced the dependency table in §14.6.)
    2. Coverage pass. Every topic list in the brief was traced to a specific section (§16.3).
    3. Practice pass. Every chapter has L1–L4 exercises, every part has a checkpoint, and every part from Part II on has at least one project.

    Mechanical consistency checks (run by the generator for Sections 11–13): chapter numbering is contiguous (1–99), section numbering is contiguous inside every chapter, every chapter folder matches its chapter number, and every part has a folder and a roadmap stage.

    16.4 Additions beyond the brief, and why

    Addition Why it earns its place
    Three-Book structure with a marked "Essential core complete" point Lets readers stop at job-ready without feeling unfinished
    Reading paths A–E Real readers arrive with different backgrounds; checkpoints make skipping safe
    The five threads and the TaskFlow running project Cohesion: readers see the same ideas and domain mature
    Ch 5.6 reading compiler errors + Appendix C The #1 practical barrier for TypeScript beginners
    Ch 35 typing the DOM + P09 vanilla app Makes "Why React?" experiential, and grounds React's event and ref types
    Ch 33 error handling across layers Error design is a core professional skill the brief mentioned only in passing
    Ch 60 state architecture and Ch 62 server state The most common real-world React mistake is putting server data in client state
    Ch 66 types vs tests as a model Answers the brief's question with a reusable mental model
    Ch 96 frameworks and Server Components Modern React work increasingly happens in frameworks; the serialization boundary is a runtime-safety topic
    Ch 97 team practices (Essential) Code review and conventions are daily work for every professional
    De-abstraction exercises Practicing removing abstractions is the strongest defense against over-engineering
    Generated TOC, tree, and index Keeps the curriculum's structure consistent as it evolves

    16.6 Known risks and how the design handles them

    Risk Mitigation
    Version drift (TypeScript, React, tooling) Concepts are version-independent; version-specific details live in 🆕/🕰 sidebars; examples are compiled in CI (§12.7), so drift shows up as failing builds
    Tool churn (bundlers, test runners, schema libraries) Each tool is chosen with stated reasons and named alternatives (§1.7, Appendix H); concepts are taught before tools (e.g., the hand-rolled useQuery before TanStack Query)
    Length (99 chapters) Three Books, tiers, reading paths, and checkpoints let readers take the shortest valid route
    Learner drop-off at the hard jumps Sawtooth difficulty, consolidation weeks, extra exercises at the eight jumps (§14.3–14.5)
    Over-engineering by enthusiastic learners Every advanced chapter pairs power with "when not to", and the rubric scores simplicity

    16.7 Verdict

    The curriculum is complete with respect to the brief: every requested topic is mapped to a teaching location (§16.3), every review criterion has a documented fix (§16.2), and every chapter has practice while every part has a checkpoint. It also goes beyond the brief where real-world professional work demands it (§16.4).

    The design choices that matter most:

    1. Problem before solution, everywhere. Even React is introduced through the reader's own pain log.
    2. The compile-time/runtime boundary is a thread, not a chapter. It is the book's most important idea, and it is revisited in eight places.
    3. Mastery is optional, and clearly labeled as optional. The Essential core stands on its own, and Book Three answers questions the core made the reader ask.
    4. Projects are a ladder, not a pile. The project ladder runs from P01 to the capstones.
